speechtext: Before the Oi-ders of the Day are called, I want to refer to reports that have appeared, particularly in some of the newspapers belonging to the party of the opposition. It is stated in these papers that I initiated the debate on stock speculation the day before yesterday for the purpose of assisting the government to take up time while we were waiting for their railway policy. I need hai-dly say that such intention never entered my mind. I might not have referred to the matter wei-e it not that the same opinion was expressed by the leader of the opposition yesterday in the House. On the same day on which I made the motion, another hon. gentleman, during my absence from the House, the member for West Toronto, stated plainly that the government had succeeded in getting one of their followers to waste another afternoon.
Do you refer to me ?

To the hon. member for West Toronto.
Mi-. CLARKE. I represent West Toronto.
Mi-. BOURASSA. Then it is a mistake in Hansard.' I mean Mr. Osier. But, coming from that gentleman, I would not mind the charge : I know where the shoe pinched him. As far as the hon. leader of the opposition is concerned, I think our personal relations are such that I might appeal to the fairness of that hon. gentleman. I can tell him that members of the government have trouble enough with me in connection with their government business that they would never think of asking me to do that which it has been suggested I have done ; and I would be the last man to enter into such a compact.

Let me say t">
my hon. friend that I would accept most

freely and fully any assurance from liim either in the House or out of the House. What I said yesterday was that we were marking time because my hon. friend proposed a resolution from which, with all deference to his views, I did not think that very much practical good would come, although I quite recognized his desire to bring about an improvement in the conditions to which his resolution had reference. STRIKE OF EMPLOYEES OF CANADA FOUNDRY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Labour if any representations have been made to him in regard to the trouble existing in Toronto between the Canada Foundry Company and the iron moulders of that city ? According to the press of that city, it appears that matters are in a very serious condition, the company being represented as bringing out a large contingent from the old country evidently to take the places of the strikers, and that the men are now making arrangements to be taken back. I would like to know if any representations have been made to the Department of Labour on the subject ?

subtopic: STRIKE OF EMPLOYEES OF CANADA FOUNDRY COMPANY.
speechtext: That subject was discussed for two hours last night.

subtopic: STRIKE OF EMPLOYEES OF CANADA FOUNDRY COMPANY.
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Smith, Vancouver), I would say that the department has received no communication from any person in reference to the strike in question. The strike is a somewhat serious one, and as has just been mentioned by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) was the subject of a reference in the House last night. Neither party having applied to the department for intervention, it is a question whether any proffer of intervention would be acceptable. However, it was pressed upon the attention of the government that the department should proffer its services, and having considered that suggestion, I have given instructions to the department to have a communication directed to the representatives of the different interests offering the services of the department. Whether or not they will be accepted, or if accepted they will be productive of any good, is a matter the future only can tell, but the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) said last night-I do not know his source of information-that as far as the Foundry Company were concerned, they were not free
agents in the matter, and could not withdraw without the consent of some other union, I think some American union. However, that would be for them to consider in ease they are willing to accept the services of the department.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during my absence last evening, reference was made to a case of some importance. I refer to the case of the steamer * Scotia ' in connection with certain salvage services which were rendered by the Anchor Line steamer ' Furnessia.' I deem the matter of sufficient importance to make a special statement of the government's connection
