speechtext:
Todd, of New York, representing the Anchor Line, called to see me to-day, and we discussed very fully the situation with regard to these proceedings. He agreed with me that It would probably be useless to sue the insurers or builders while the present judgment of the supreme court of Newfoundland, holding the Crown exempt from salvage charges remains in force, and we also agreed that negotiations with the insurers under present conditions would probably not be hopeful. I told Mr. Todid that the government, except for its guarantees from the insurers and builders would not have raised the question as to exemption of Crown property from payment for salvage services, but would no doubt have submitted to the jurisdiction of the court and paid
whatever amount might finally have been awarded for these services, and that the Crown wias practically forced into the position which it has taken by reason of the attitude of the insurers, who set up our exemption and refused to admit our claim for damages. We agreed, therefore, that Mr. Todd should recommend the company to proceed with the appeal and have it brought on for hearing if possible early in July. I stated on the part of the government that we would appear and submit the facts as they stand to the court, stating as above that we set up the point of exemption to protect ourselves as against the insurers. If the company succeed on the appeal, of course we will have to pay the company for the salvage services, and afterwards have our recourse against the insurers or builders. If the Crown succeeds upon the appeal it will still be open for the company to make such representations for the consideration of the government as it may be advised with a view to obtaining indemnity upon the merits of the case. Meantime a letter is to be written to the English solicitors who have charge of the claim against the insurers, instructing them to notify the insurers that the appeal will go on unless they make a satisfactory settlement ; that the Crown as a defence would admit the salvors' claim and pay such amount as might be adjudged ; that in the circumstances we hope that the insurers will abandon the claim that the Crown is exempt and agree to the (payment of reasonable damages. Otherwise that while looking to them, not only for the damages, but also the costs which we may have to pay as the res,tilts of the litigation. Our solicitors are to be instructed to effect a settlement with the insurers with the concurrence of the salvors if possible. and to report the result of their negotiations. but in the absence of any agreement with the insurers the appeal is to proceed.
There the matter stands at the present time.

House again in committee on Bill jNo. 200) respecting the Inspection and Sale of Seeds.-The Minister of Agriculture.
On section 4.

When this Bill was in committee before, it was the subject of a good deal of discussion in general as well as in detail, and there were suggestions from both sides of the House with regard to its provisions. On its first introduction, I pointed out that I was not wedded by any means to the details, and that I would be very glad to receive suggestions and to see if these suggestions could be incorporated in the Bill without marring any of its essential principles. As a result of that discussion and consideration of it, I intend to submit certain amendments which I may read together as they are more or less dependent the one upon the other. Section 1, of the Bill provides that it shall come into force the 1st day of September this year, and I propose to substitute for that the 1st day of July next year. This will give those who are engaged in the seed trade an opportunity of disposing of the seeds which

they have on hand, which they purchased not knowing that there would be such a law as this. It will also he time enough to bring about the improvement in the sale of seeds for next year. Then I would propose that in clause 3 the word ' vegetables ' should be struck out. I believe that in the future the trade in seeds of vegetables and flowers will have to come under the operation of an Act similiar to this by the demand of the people themselves ; but, at the present time it is possible that greater difficulties might arise in dealing with the trade in these seeds than those which we encounter in dealing with the trade in ordinary agricultural seeds. The menace to agriculture is much greater from the present position of trade in ordinary agricultural seeds than it is from the condition of trade in vegetable or garden seeds. I am therefore going to propose that the word ' vegetable ' be struck out of section 3, which would remove that difficulty from the Bill.
Then, I think it would be best that section 4 should not apply to export trade. I therefore propose to introduce into the second line of that section, after the word ' sale,' the words ' for the purpose of seeding in the Dominion of Canada.' That would make the provisions of the section, in regard to the marking and grading of seeds, not applicable to seeds intended for export. I think that eventually, in the course of a little time, it will be requisite to make that clause of the Act and those dependent upon it apply to the export trade as well as the home trade; but, as I have always wished, in dealing with this Bill, to proceed slowly, and to make the improvements step by step, I am disposed to meet the objection raised in regard to that point and to provide that section 4 shall only apply, for the present at afiy rate, to the home trade.
I would like to deal in section 6 with another exemption or partial exemption to the provisions of this Act. A good deal of discussion arose in regard to a supposed transaction between two farmers in a neighbourhood, one of whom raises an ordinary crop of seeds and sells it to his neighbour, as farmers frequently do. There was a very evident desire expressed by many members of the House that the provisions of the Act should not apply to such a transaction. Some members, however, believed that they should. I confess that I think the principles of the Act should apply to a transaction of that kind. But if there are difficulties in the way, which would prevent the proper enforcement of the Act without great hardship, I would be glad to adopt any amendment that would meet that case. I asked the hon. gentlemen who engaged in the former discussion to suggest an amendment for that purpose. No practical suggestion, I think, was then made; but after thinking over the matter and discussing it with my officers, I have a suggestion to make which I think will perhaps accomplish Hon. Mr. FISHER.
the object in view and at the same time not make the Act inoperative. 1 am going to propose an additional subsection as subsection ' e ' to section 6, providing that the Act shall not apply :
Or to seed that is grown and sown by any farmer on his own premises unless the purchaser of such seed demands from the seller at the time of the sale thereof that the said seed be supplied to him subject to the provisions of this Act.
That would leave on the purchaser the onus of requiring that the transaction should be subject to the provisions of this Act. If the purchaser wishes the transaction to be subject to the provisions of this Act, he can require it; if he does not so require it, then the provisions of the Act will not apply to the transaction, and nobody else can attack the seller, even though the seeds and the package in which they were placed might not fulfil the provisions of this Act. I think that meets the views of those gentlemen who thought the Act was too severe upon farmers who sold seeds to their neighbours, while at the same time it puts into the hands of the purchaser the privilege, if he chooses to exercise it, of having the provisions of this Act applied to the transaction. It seems to me to be a solution of the difficulty pointed out as possible to occur, and at the same time complies with the spirit and the general principle of the Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: Suppose the purchaser said to the seller, I wish to get from you No. 1 red clover, and purchased accordingly, and said nothing about other provisions of the Act. Would not that bring the transaction under this Act ?

If the purchaser wished to avail himself of this section, he would have to do so, and then every provision of the Act would apply. It is not intended that the purchaser should be able to apply one provision of the Act and not another. If the purchaser wished the transaction to be subject to the provisions of the Act he would have to say so at the time of the transaction. If he did say so, then the whole transaction would be subject to the provisions of the Act. If he did not make that stipulation at the time of the purchase, the provisions of the Act would not apply, and the seller of the seeds would not be liable to be prosecuted under the Act. That, I believe, to be a fair and equitable solution of the difficulty suggested.
That applies to all classes of seeds ?

Yes. Of course there are some provisions of the Act which apply to some seeds and others to other seeds ; but that would not change these provisions. The next difficulty that arose was in connection with section 7. Exception was taken to the amount of the fine, and the suggestion was made that there ought to be separate fines

-one for the first offence and the other for second and subsequent offences. That seemed to be reasonable, and I propose to substitute in place of section 7 a section providing a fine jiot exceeding $25 and not less than $5 for the first offence, and not exceeding $50 and not less than $10 for the second offence, together with the costs of the prosecution. Objection was taken on the part of the wholesale dealers that they might be held liable for the contents of the package after it had gone into the hands of the retailer or any other person and its contents had been tampered with. To avoid any such possibility, I am proposing a clause providing that the package shall be sealed, and as long as the seal is unbroken the party who sold it shall be liable for the contents. If it should be broken, he may be still held liable, provided that, in the presence of two disinterested witnesses, a sample of the contents is put into another sealed package.
What is to prevent the duplicating of the seal ? Are you providing for that contingency ?
I have not thought of that. That would probably be an infringement of the Trades Marks Act. Some provision would be necessary to complete the protection given the seller.
How is a retail merchant going to get samples without breaking the seal ?

When the seal is broken, the wholesale dealer is no longer responsible, but the retail merchant may take a sample from the bag and put it into another receptacle under seal, in the presence of two disinterested witnesses, and the contents of the bag would be judged by this sample. I propose to amend section 12 to meet the objections of the seed merchants, who seem to think it is not clear enough. This section provides for samples to be sent within seven days to any official analyst of seeds, taken from any seeds which are found or suspected to be sold in violation of the provisions of this Act. Section 15 provides that one-half of the pecuniary penalty shall be payable to the informant or the complainant. This section was struck out by the committee, and I would suggest that in its place the following section be inserted
Any pecuniary penalty imposed under this Act shall when recovered be payable one half to the imformant when such informant or complainant is the purchaser of the seed with respect to which the penalty is imposed, in all other cases the whole penalty shall be payable to His Majesty.
A man may purchase a very small quantity merely in order that he may be in a position to prosecute and realize half the fine.

Such a case might occur. But, if the sale has really been made, I think the penalty ought to be inflicted. A man buys a small quantity of seed, say even eight or ten pounds of clover or timothy, and he finds afterwards that the seed is not what it is purported to be. It is very considerable trouble to him, and often very considerable expense, to prosecute. The ordinary individual has not a sufficiently high sense of public duty to prosecute. But if we throw upon the purchaser the onus and responsibility of prosecuting I think that when a man renders such a public service, it is only fair that he should have a portion of the result.

I think the intention is good, and it would be all right in the case of a legitimate buyer that the person who prosecutes should receive half the fine. But the hon. minister will admit that under the section as he proposes it a person might buy a very small quantity, and, on the strength of the purchase, prosecute and secure half the fine.

I understand that, yet I do not see how we can discriminate between one purchaser and another. But this clause is to prevent third parties prosecuting. A farmer might purchase seed and not wish to prosecute, and a third party, through malice or through hope of pecuniary advantage, might enter an action without any personal interest in the transaction at all. I wish to prevent that. I find that section 17, which provides for an appeal is not necessary, for the provisions of the Summary Convictions Act will apply. And, as it is not necessary, its presence in the Bill might involve technical legal difficulties. I shall, therefore, propose to strike out section 17. These are the amendments, that, after careful consideration of the arguments advanced in a former discussion, commend themselves to my mind, and I think their adoption will make the Bill as perfect as it is possible to make in a first attempt in legislation of this kind. When the Bill was up for discussion before, I took occasion to say that we had in the committee the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Bruce) who has had much experience in this trade, and I trusted that before the passage of the Bill the committee would have the advantage of his advice and assistance in discussing it. I hope he will give the committee his views, as he did when he presented a deputation of the seedsmen to myself as minister in charge of the Bill. If a general discussion is desired, I would ask hon. members to proceed, and then we can take up the clauses.

I should suppose the minister would leave the matter for a day or two until the members of the committee have had an opportunity to look into the amendments he has suggested. I- understand that

It is not in accordance with the usual procedure of the House that such amendments should be proceeded with until after reasonable notice; and while I would not be disposed to insist upon that in opposition to the hon. minister's wish, I must confess that I find it difficult to follow the amendments as read, because of the difficulty of hearing liim. I think members will be glad to consider the amendments as they will find them in ' Hansard ' to-morrow before attempting to proceed with them in detail.

It will perhaps be better to proceed with the general discussion, and some explanations may be called for. My bon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) did ask an explanation which I asked leave to postpone until I had gone through the amendments. I think it would be well to have a discussion before we proceed, as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) sugests.

I referred to the faet that we make a time limit, which, I take it, involves the putting of a1 date on the seal. If the time limit is near expiring and the seed were sold to an innocent party-as the Minister of Agriculture is engaged at this moment, I shall wait until he can give me his attention.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the hon. minister has gone through the amendments he proposes, I think we should take the Bill up section by section and consider the amendments as they arise ? If it is desired that further time should be given on any particular amendment, the discussion of the clause to which it relates can be postponed. In this way, we shall make some progress, but, with a general discussion we shall make no progress.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister's amendments are more important than the Bill, It would be better to have them reprinted, so that hon. members can consider them before taking up the discussion.

I was merely responding to the invitation of the minister, who intimated that it would be proper for me to refer now to the matter I mentioned, which was this:	When the seal is put on, there
must be a date, because the amendment proposes that the guarantee shall be good only for a certain length of time. If the seed passes into the hands of an innocent party about the time of the expiry of the guarantee he would practically not have any guarantee whatever.

The hon. member spoke about the date. The date must be on the seal but the object of providing that in no case shall the responsibility for such seed extend beyond ninety days of the sale thereof, which date must be plainly marked on the package or bag which contains the seed, is, that some seeds deteriorate in ninety days. That is the Mr. BELL,
case with a good many seeds, but not with all by any means. Many seeds will last much longer. That is the object of making the time ninety days.

We will suppose that a seedsman got an order for certain seeds, and the wholesale man had them on hand, but the time of that warrantee had about expired, lacking a few days.* He sold those seeds, but they did not reach the consignee until after the expiry of that time, and when he received those seeds he found they were not up to the standard, who would be responsible then? The action had not been commenced within the 90 days, and his warrantee expired by the effluxion of time.
That is a legal point that I would not like to give an opinion upon. There are many cases in Acts where a delay is fixed, and in those cases the point has to be taken up from a legal point of view.

The object in making a law is to avoid any of these technicalities that might result in litigation. It seems to me it would be possible to provide that when any person sold seeds under a warrantee, he should be held responsible for them after the time had expired before they reached the consignee.

The purchaser knows what the date of sealing was. Tbe date has to be put upon the package, and he knows what the provisions of the Act are, and therefore he knows that within a certain delay he has certain rights. After that delay has passed those rights cease.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would like the minister to explain what kind of seeds will deteriorate in 90 days.
I am informed by those who have studied this matter more than myself, that hulled timothy seed cannot be counted upon after 90 days-timothy seed that has lost its hull.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have kept timothy seed over two or three years, and it was just as good as at the begininng. I have often had it in store for two or three years. I am satisfied that timothy seed, if kept in a dry place, and unless it gets damaged by moisture, is just as good at the end of twelve months as when it is first threshed.

I think the hon. gentleman would have found, if he had had that seed tested by a seed analyst, that it had steadily deteriorated and was getting poorer every year.
air. TAYLOR. When it was sowed the result was just as good.

Any results he would observe in a field

in a particular case, would be far too inaccurate and unsatisfactory to lead to a general conclusion.

Ill regard to this Bill,
I regret to say that I was not in the House the other day when the Minister of Agriculture gave his explanations, I was otherwise engaged. I have not heard either his explanations given this afternoon. However, as I read the Bill cursorily, it seems to me that it is going to have a peculiar effect in our western country. For instance, clause 3 says :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, for the purpose of seeding, any seeds of cereals, grasses, clovers- &c., having in the packages or hags any seed of wild mustard, Russian thistle and so forth. If he does so, he is subject to a penalty running from $10 to $100. Clause 9 says that any person may go on to a farmer's premises and if lie finds any of these seeds in his sacks or bags he may bring an action and fine him $100, and get half the fine. Now, I do not believe this will work in the western portion of the country especially. It seems to me it simply means this, that if a farmer wants to change his seed, as he frequently does, and he sends to Winnipeg and buys a carload of seed, if it contains any mustard seed or any other of these seeds mentioned here, he can be fined $100. If that is the meaning of this Act, then I may say it may apply to some isolated state of affairs that may exist in some little five-acre lot where they pick the wheat out by hand, but on the prairies it means that every farmer that sells seed out there will be subject to a penalty, not a single one would escape. The idea is just about as impracticable as the one passed a few days ago about marking butter. It seems we have a lot of theorists, men running experimental farms, faddists, men who would starve on a farm of their own, and they are evolving out of their own brains some ideal state of affairs that should exist, and thev are trying to make use of this House to put it into law. The consequence is that the law remains on the statute-book without being obeyed, a dead letter, a fraud upon the public. After a while the farmers will kick and the law is repealed. Now, I merely ask the minister if the idea of this Act is that if any farmer sells seed one bag or a hundred bags, and which are found to have a few grains of mustard seed in it, he can be fined $100 at the instance of any neighbour of his, or informer who may be found around his premises. If some man who has a spite against him knows he has got 100 bushels of wheat for sale, all he has to do is to go into his barn and take one of these sacks and find a little mustard seed or Russian thistle in it, and fine him $100 and get half the fine. If that is so, then this Bill had better be stopped at once.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the committee that this whole discussion is out of order, there is nothing before the Chair. I would ask the minister to tell me what is the proposition now before the committee. There is no progress being made at all.
The government benches are obstructing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
After the minister gave an expose of the proposition which he intended to bring before the House in connection with this particular Bill, it is then the duty of the committee to take up the Bill section by section and apply the amendments proposed by the minister. But this general discussion, when there is no question before the committee at all, is wholly out of order, and I have no more control of the committee than if I were 100 miles away. Unless I am overruled by the committee, as I generally am when I am right, I would rule that this discussion is out of order. We will have to commence first by a motion to reopen all the sections which have al-readv been carried, that is, every section of the Bill with the exception of three. This discussion is on sections which have already been passed on by the committee. After a motion is carried to reconsider what we have done already, then it will be in order to more these proposed amendments to each section as we go on, and then we will be making some progress.
Mr. SPROUT,E. Might I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. minister referred to several amendments which he intended to propose to the Bill, and he asked for a general discussion upon them ? It was in following out the suggestion that we were endeavouring to refer to these various amendments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Ministers are human like the rest of us, and they are sometimes out of order like the rest of us. Therefore, I am calling the minister's attention to the rule of order. I have put about two hundred Bills through my hands this session, and there has not been one that has been put through in this irregular way.
The MINISTER OF AGRICRULTURE moved
That section two be amended by striking out the words ' first day of September, nineteen hundred and three ' and inserting in lieu thereof the words ' first day of July, nineteen hundred and four.'

Will this be on the understanding that we are to reconsider the entire sections of the Bill 1 Will the hon. minister give us that assurance, or will we have a discussion of the Bill 6n this question ?

Subject to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I

suppose that if the Bill is to go into force on a certain day the whole of the Bill might be discussed as to the advisability of its going into force on that day.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose I am in order now. I need hardly say that in this Bill there is the promise of a great deal of good to the farmers of this country, but I am satisfied In the House we have not amongst us the commercial experience necessary to make this Bill perfect. I have been approached when at home toy the retailers of seeds, who say that they have not had an opportunity of expressing their views, and that in the amendments which have been suggested by the wholesale trade they have relieved themselves of a certain share of responsibility by shouldering it off upon the retail dealers. One of the largest retail dealers told me that rather than carry on the seed business under the Bill as proposed to the House, he would go out of business. I would suggest, in the interests of the farmers at large, that we should perfect this Bill as far as we are able and then let it go to the various agricultural societies, retail dealers' associations and wholesale dealers in seeds, and let them consider it and suggest amendments. After that we will be in possession of such an array of facts as will enable us to perfect a Bill which will be of use to the country. We all know the injury that is being inflicted through the sale of impure seeds. I am satisfied that the lion. Minister of Agriculture has the welfare of the agricultural community at heart in bringing forward this Bill, but a Bill so far-reaching in its consequences ought to be considered with reference to the trade it affects, and especially with reference to the interests of the farmer who grows seed and grows it for the purpose of selling it. I do not think we have that commercial knowledge of the seed business which will enable us to perfect a Bill that will be just in all its particulars to every class of the community, and therefore I say that we should try to perfect this Bill, to adopt the suggestions that are made by the hou. minister, who has given a great deal of care to it, and then leave it to be further considered by the wholesale trade, the retail trade and the farmers, and give them an opportunity for making suggestions in regard to it, so that when we come to consider it next year we will toe able to perfect a Bill that will be applicable to all classes of the community and that will operate for the welfare of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I was going to make the suggestion that has been made by the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) in regard to this Bill.
I do not think that the farming community or the seedsmen of the country, those who handle and do nothing else, are sufficiently familiar with the provisions of the measure to understand

them properly. The seedsmen and farmers are entirely with the hon. minister in his desire to improve the quality of the seed production of Canada. We are all much interested in bringing about this result as he is, and we will do everything we possibly can to achieve the object w'hich he expects to result from this Bill. But we have not yet had sufficient time to consider the Bill or to understand how it would operate as a mercantile measure. I would suggest that the hon. minister should continue the work of educating the farmers at the institute meetings which has been going on for some years past, and he might possibly also issue a bulletin giving his views in regard to the intended legislation that we are considering here to-day. During the recess the seedsmen of the country and the experts of the Department of Agriculture might consider the Bill and agree upon such provisions as would not be an injury to the farmers or interfere too much with the seedsmen in the management of their business. I understand perfectly well that it is not the intention of the hon. minister to inflict any hardship upon either the farmers or the seedsmen, and if time were given for the consideration of the matter between now and the next meeting of the House. I think a Bill might be brought in that would be of service to the country, and which would realize the expectations of the hon. minister in regard to our seed product.

I took a copy of this Bill home and submitted it to one of our seedsmen, and the conclusion he reached was very much the same as that of the seedsman to whom the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) referred, that if this Bill became law' he would have to go out of business, because he thought it quite impossible to carry on his business and keep within the provisions of the law. He said that the law' must either be a dead letter or there must toe constant and repeated violation of it, which no seedsman would desire to have. The opinion I expressed when the Bill was first proposed, and the opinion which I hold still, is that unless the Bill is very much amended it w'ill be utterly impossible for any seedsman to carry on his business without finding himself in trouble and liable to prosecution.
It seems to me that the proposition of the hon. minister, which, if I understand it aright, is to postpone the effect of the Bill for another year, meets all the arguments that have been put forward.
No.

It must be taken for granted that the hon. minister and the department have given the matter some expert attention, and that the Bill in its present shape has certainly the principle to commend it, and that there is valuable information as to details. At the same time,

we can all recognize that it is a Bill of very far-reacliing effect, and that probably it would not be well for it to go into effect without everybody having a say m regard to it. If the Bill is not to go into effect until after the next session of parliament, then the best way to call the attention of the people of Canada to it is to put it on the statute-book. I strongly support the Bill, with the amendment proposed by the Minister of Agriculture.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) This Bill will not come into operation before the first of July, 1904, and why should we be in a hurry to pass it at all this session. Let it be circulated so that those who are interested in it may understand it thoroughly, and then next session we will be able to consider the objections offered to it and will be in a position to pass a better Bill. Among the many faults we have in this House, one is that we pass too much legislation on subjects that might as well be left alone to regulate themselves.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If this Bill is to pass, the word ' person ' should be struck out and the word ' dealer ' inserted. We know it to be a fact that farmers in the North-west and in all parts of the country keep oats, barley, and wheat, for seeding purposes, and give them to their neighbours. If a farmer has any such weed as mustard in his crop and if he sells the seed to his neighbour he is liable to be prosecuted under this Bill. In fact if the Bill passes no one dare sell his neighbour a bushel of oats or any other grain if he had a noxious weed in his fields, and you will hardly get a farm in Ontario that "will not show some of the weeds mentioned in the Act. If you pass the Bill at all it should apply to dealers only and not to farmers.

If it be true as the hon. member for Leeds says that every farm in Ontario is flooded with weeds, then it is a strong argument in favour of this Bill, the principle of which is to check the evil of weeds in our cultivated lands.

This Bill does not come into force until after next session, and it is much better that we should hold it over and make whatever amendments we think are desirable then rather than to pass it now and amend it afterwards. If we hold it over and pass all its provisions at once without amendment then it will be plain so that ordinary mortals may understand it.

The question arises whether we should make this Bill law this year or leave it oyer until next session, but in either case it is much better that we should try to make the Bill as perfect as possible, now that it is before the House. My hon. friend from Brant suggested that we should discuss it and then submit it to farmers institutes and agricultural meetings. If it does not become law this year it ought to be so submitted, but if it is to be submitted it ought be submitted in as perfect a shape as possible. We are legislating here on a new subject and one which I know involves great difficulty, but we have been able to legislate successfully on new subjects in the past and there is no reason why we should not do so in this case. The hon. gentleman from Leeds says that the amendments amount to as much as the whole Bill. That is not the case, but even if it were it would be no objection to the measure. What I want to find, and what the majority of this committee want to find is a solution of the difficulties which the farmers of Canada now labour under in their purchase of seeds for seeding purposes. This committee has almost unanimously accepted the principle of the Bill, and if it is desirable that such a Bill should become law then the condition of affairs in the country is acknowledged to be such that the time is ripe for its enactment. My hon. friend from Hamilton said that the seed dealers who think that they are more aimed at in this Bill than any one else, are quite prepared to acknowledge the principle of this Bill, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) said that the Bill should be limited to dealers. I may say that the dealers already think that the Bill almost aims exclusively at them. I do not think that is the case, but their view has to be taken into consideration. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) has attacked the Bill on very broad grounds and he has said that it is entirely unworkable especially in the North-west Territories. My hon. friend is not aware probably that in the North-west Territories there is local legislation which is far more strict than the provisions of this Bill.
It is not carried out.

It may not be carried out for the benefit of the people, but, nevertheless the representatives of the people have adopted such legislation. If the hon. gentleman is surprised at it, it is simply because he has not taken the trouble to study the question, and has made statements to the House without knowing the details of the question he has been talking about. The hon. gentleman may be perfectly right in what he says. It may be that this Bill is unworkable in the North-west Territories ; but the representatives of the people elected in the Northwest Territories believe that more drastic legislation is necessary, and I suppose that when they put it on the statute-book, they believed that it was workable, and in the interest of the people of the North-west Territories. I do not know the North-west Territories and Manitoba as well as the hon. gentleman does ; but I do know them well enough to know that if there is any part of the Dominion of Canada that requires

legislation with regard to the purity of seeds and the destruction of weeds, it is Manitoba and the North-west Territories. But the provisions of this Bill have been, as my hon. friend from Alberta says, the subject of the utmost consideration and investigation, not only by myself as minister, but by the experts employed in my department to deal especially with this subject. I may say that the provisions of this Bill, as it stands to-day, are not nearly as drastic and stringent as the condition of affairs in the country would lead us to believe would be advisable ; but I understand perfectly well that what is advisable may not be feasible, and that we have to creep before we can run ; and therefore we are obliged to minimize the restrictive character of the Bill to such an extent that it may be fairly workable and may attain the objects we have in view. It is for that reason that I decided to-day to propose certain amendments to the Bill, and I would be glad to have the co-operation and assistance of the committee on each amendment.

With regard to the ordinance which the hon. minister says is on the statute-book of the North-west Territories, I have not seen such an ordinance. If there is such an ordinance, it certainly has never been observed since the day it was passed; because there is not a farmer in Manitoba or the North-west Territories who could carry out the provisions of section 3 of this Act. If the North-west legislature was foolish enough to put on the statute-book an Act which could never be carried out, I hope we are not foolish enough to repeat that Act in this House. In the Northwest Territories, in Manitoba, in Minnesota, in Dakota, or in any of the other states which produce large quantities of grain, such an Act could not possibly be enforced. If the minister wants to suit the farmers, let this Act be considered by them. If he wants to suit the seed dealers, he is quite right to pass such legislation. For instance, if section 3. which provides that no person shall seli seeds unless they are entirely free from the seeds of the weeds named in the section, were modified to say that they shall contain not more than 10 per cent or 5 per cent or some other per centage of these seeds, it might to a certain extent be workable. The hon. gentleman also wants to take into consideration the fact that when a farmer buys his seed, he usually puts it through a process of blue-stoning before he puts it into the ground, and provision might be made for imposing that duty on the seller of the seed as well. The minister before passing this Act, should consult the farmers of the prairies as well as the seed dealers of the east. As the Bill stands, it would be a grass hardship on the farmers of the west. It would i>ut the farmer into the hands of some unprincipled scoundrel, who could go into his granary and pick some of these Hon. Mr. FISHER.
deleterious seeds out of his stock, and then have him hauled up and fined $100, and, if he did not pay the fine, have him sent to jail ; and, if the farmer wanted to put the man out of his granary, he might subject himself to another fine of $500. I submit that the clause giving the informer the power to enforce the penalty is wrong. That should be put into the hands of a government official, who would not get any part of the fine. 'There is scarcely a police magistrate who does not reflect severely on the character of whiskey informers, and these informers would be in the same category. If the minister is going to enforce the Bill or bring it up again next session, I think it should be modified in the ways I have suggested.

My hon. friend evidently has not studied tlie Bill or listened to what I have said this afternoon. He. says the Bill has not been submitted to the farmers of the Northwest Territories. The details of the Bill of course have not been submitted to them, but the question the Bill deals with was brought up and discussed last winter at every institute held in the North-west Territories. With regard to the farmer selling seed to another farmer, the amendment which I read to the House to-day, providing that the provisions of this Act shall not apply to such a transaction unless the purchaser at the time requires that it shall be subject to the provisions of the Act, meets that case; so that if two neighbours wish to sell seed to each other without being subject to the provisions of this Act, they can do so. The hon. gentleman also objected to the informer getting a portion of the fine. That also is proposed to be modified. That section of the Bill was struck out at the previous meeting of the committee, but I propose to insert in place of it another section providing that when such Informant is the purchaser of the seed with respect to which the penalty is imposed, then and then only shall he get one-half of the penalty. A person who is not the purchaser would have no chance of getting any portion of the penalty ; but the man who has suffered a wrong, and who takes the trouble, not to right his own wrong, but to do a service to the community, ought to have something for the public service he has rendered. He ought to have a portion of the fine to reimburse him for the trouble he has taken, in a public spirited way-because probably the wrong he has suffered does not amount to much-to put a stop to the selling of inferior seed.

I do not think that much harm will result if the Bill be allowed to stand over another year. Let copies be sent to the farmers institutes and
farmers' associations and the grangers, and we will then next session know what the farmers think of it. There is no great hurry for the Bill. We have lived all these years

without it, and can get along without it another year.

X approve of the hon. minister's present intention of not putting the Bill into force this year. But I would go further still and let the discussion stand over until next session. I do not think that the public mind mind has been directed to this matter to any great extent. No doubt the hon. minister has given it a good deal of thought and has an honest desire to provide a remedy for what he considers a grievance, but nevertheless it seems to me, as I said the other day, that we are erring on the side of too much legislation and do not recognize the ability of our people to regulate many of these matters themselves. There is very good reason why we should defer further consideration of this measure. I understand the government to say that they are exceedingly anxious to get certain important measures before the House without delay ; and if we go into a discussion of tnis matter, we will be putting an obstacle in the way of progress. There is another and a more serious difficulty.
. If this Bill is persisted in, I fear we will witness another of those ruptures which are becoming alarmingly frequent this session. It is evident that we are on the verge of an unfortunate friction between the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) and the hon. Minister of Agriculture, I would deeply regret that anything of the kind should occur at this juncture. The government is already sufficiently embarrassed without having the further embarrassment of one of its ministers being attacked by a prospective minister. We can make every allowance for the language used by the hon. member for Selkirk with regard to the hon. minister, because he has just come from a scene of agitation and disappointment and finds it difficult to restrain his feelings. As to the fitness of the language, I have nothing to say.
Has this anything to do with clause 2 ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, it has not.

I hope that I shall keep myself within the rules of the House. I wish simply to express my sincere hope that at the present juncture, when the friction now existing among hon. members opposite, both in the cabinet and out of it, threatens to bring about such a state of things that we may have no administration at all, the hon. minister will see the advisability of not pressing this measure. Speaking in all earnestness, I believe that it is not in the interest of the seedsmen or farmers that we should commit ourselves to any definite policy such as is laid down in this Bill. The matter, having been brought to the attention of the public, should be allowed to stand over until another session, when it
can be put into such shape that it will be more likely to give general satisfaction and probably, by the time another session comes around, the hon. minister will be relieved from the responsibilities of office and not have to father the measure at all.

I represent a rural constituency, Mr. Chairman, and there are some things in connection with this debate which I find rather puzzling. I have always been under the impression that the farmer raised the seed which he sold the dealer. We have some noxious weeds in our county; and while I am as much the friend of the farmer as anybody else, I fail to understand why, if you do not punish the farmer who raised the dirty seed and sells it to the dealer, you should punish the dealer for selling this dirty seed furnished him by the farmer.

The seedsmen of Canada are not asking for this legislation, but as the hon. Minister of Agriculture has introduced the Bill, we desire to see it passed in such a shape that it will be as little harmful as possible both to the farmers and seedsmen. To show you, Sir, that the country is not suffering to any alarming extent I shall take the liberty of reading some remarks which Dr. Saunders made when giving his evidence before the Agricultural Committee on the 12th of June. Dr. Saunders stated that 131 samples of clover seed which he tested averaged seventy-five per cent in germinating power, and seventy-five samples of timothy seed averaged eighty-three percent ; showing that in these important and staple seeds, although we may meet with an occasional poor sample, the Canadian seedsmen have supplied farmers with a very reliable quality of the seed, and that most of the samples have been remarkably clean. This shows that we are not likely to have any greater difficulty with regard to weeds than we have had, heretofore and that the country will not suffer if we allow the Bill to stand over until the farmers and seedsmen understand it better and are better able to suggest the changes necessary to make it effective.

As a dealer in seeds for the last thirty-two years, I think I have the right to say something on the subject. If there is any question in this country that demands legislation, it is the selling of impure seeds. Our friends of the law may not be aware that last winter during three or four months, in the province of Ontario, at meeting of farmers' institute held in every section, the burden of the lectures was the fact that so many foul seeds are sold to the farmers in the grain which they buy for seed. At every one of these meetings a large chart was put up on the wall showing the places where seeds were purchased and the percentage of foul seeds in them. Every farmer present at the institute meeting, without a. single exception, said something should be done in the way of legislation in order to remedy the evil. So, I cannot see how any one can say in this House that the subject has not been before the farmers or that they have not had an opportunity to say anything about it. It is true they may not have come here with any one delegated to say these things for them, but it is a certain fact that the matter has been before them at every farmers' institute meeting, and with unanimous voice they have said that something should be done. If we do not take any action this session, all the trouble that we have been to and all me time that we have spent will be lost, and all the things that have been said here to-day and other days will have to be said next session. It is time we should settle down to work and see if we cannot get; a Bill into shape that it may be placed before the farmers' institute for discussion. Then, if there are changes to be made, we can make them. But for goodness sake let us do something, and not be staying here all the time talking.
Mr, ROSS (Ontario). The amendment is to provide that this Act shall not come into force until the 1st July, 1904. I 'think that in the previous debate in connection with the Bill, I expressed myself as believing that this measure should not come into force during this parliament, or, until next year at any rate. I think it would be wise to have it as a measure that might be legislated on at a future session, that it should practically serve as a notice of motion to the country that the matter was going to be dealt with by this parliament. The reasons advanced by the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) I think, are extremely good-that the country may have notice during the next twelve months of what they may expect in connection with the seed Bill.
I scarcely think the hon. members of this House are aware of the enormous waste there is in this country owing to noxious weeds, not only in seeds, but in cereals of all kinds. I know that we have unloaded at our elevator No. 1 Manitoba hard wheat that has a very large percentage of weed seeds. I was really surprised to see it.
7229	JULY 23, 1903	7230
And I have been told by some who are engaged in the trade that there have been some remarkable turnouts of weed seeds in the shipments of Manitoba wheat. As the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) has said, you have but to travel through the country on train to see hundreds and hundreds, even many thousands of acres of wild mustard spread before you. No one can deny that every spear of wild mustard is displacing a spear of wheat or other grain. The positive waste that is going on year after year in growing and gathering these seeds is incalculable. The province of Ontario to which I belong, has recognized this as an evil. They have declared that these noxious weeds shall not be grown on the highways or even on the fields. They give power, as I understand it, to municipalities to see to the enforcement of the law. The result is that the law is not enforced, but stands upon the statute-book practically a dead letter. If the Jbill now before us will meet the difficulty and lead to the production of a purer quality of seeds, it is of the utmost importance and in the right direction. But I believe with the hon. member for Brant and some other hon. members, that it would be better not to make a law now, but, as I say, to let this serve as a notice of motion for next session of parliament. We have a great competitor in the growing of seed in the country to the south of us. Sixty-five per cent, in round numbers of their exports, which amount to about $1,300,000,000 consists of the products of the farm. Of this, a large proportion is seeds, and the seeds grown in that country come in direct competition with the seeds grown in Canada.
We are the largest producers and exporters of aisike in the world. We are no small producers of red clover, and fairly large producers of timothy. These seeds are produced largely in the western states, in Wisconsin, Iowa, Minnesota, and I think. Indiana. They have, as I understand, no law regarding seeds.- Now, it strikes me that perhaps if we put too rigorous a law upon the trade of this country, which has been well developed by the seedsmen, it may affect our exportation of seeds out of the country. That is what appeals to (me. For myself, I have not sufficient information to form an opinion with regard to that matter, as to how we would meet the export trade of the United States in these seeds where we especially come into competition with them. Of course, we come into competition with them in our wheat, oats, barley, and those things, and also in seeds. A good many of the seeds imported into this country are used in Ontario. Under these circumstances. I can agree with the proposition which has been made by several hon. members here to-day fo let this Bill serve as a notice to the country that next year absolutely a Bill will come up for the purpose of regulating the seed
trade. In the meantime, let the farmers' institutes and dealers of all kinds be consulted in regard to it, and let them be told to suggest any amendments they choose. Another feature of the Bill that I do not agree with is that regarding the payment of the fine. It is repugnant to me that we should pass any Act here with a penalty clause which gives to the informant one-half or one-quarter of the fine, or any part of it. I thoroughly believe that all fines should go to the Crown, and that the Crown should itself enforce the Act. I know that a great many people have a serious objection to that mode of proceeding. The only department of the government where that principle may perhaps be justified, is the customs. There it may be necessary, but I say we should avoid as far as possible introducing that principle into any other Bill.

I believe this Bill is in the right direction. I am sorry that I cannot agree with the last speaker (Mr. Ross, Ontario), who thinks the Bill should not become law now. If there is an evil in this country, as it is clear we have in this respect, where bad seed is being scattei'ed broadcast over the country, why should we allow the dealers another year to get rid of that seed by placing it on the market? I think the sooner this Bill becomes law the better, and I think it should be placed upon the statute-book this year.
Moved to amend section 4 by inserting after the word ' sale ' in the 22nd line, the words, ' for the purpose of seeding within the Dominion of Canada.'
How are you going to establish that fact ? If a man has such seed, upon whom will rest the responsibility of showing that it is for the purpose of seeding in the Dominion of Canada?

When he holds seed in his warehouse or place of business, it will be held to be for sale in the Dominion of Canada. If, however, it is exported, the bill of lading which he sends forward will show that it is for export and not for sale in the Dominion of Canada. Until he takes positive steps to export it, the seed will be held to be for sale in the Dominion of Canada.
Amendment agreed to.

There were two amendments to be added to section 6. One of them, subsection (c), was carried the other day. Now, I propose another one as subsection (d), which is to meet the view expressed the other day that a farmer might desire to sell to his neighbour. This is to protect him in such transaction, but where the purchaser desires to have the provisions of the Act apply, he will have a right to express such

desire, and the provisions of the Act will apply.
Mi-. GILMOUR. I think he should ask in writing for the statutory seed.
I do not think we need imply in the law that it need be put in writing, but after being considered if it is thought necessary by tlie law department I will be glad to make such a provision.

If a person is made liable to be fined, I think the evidence against him should be perfectly clear, that he contravened the law, and in this case it could only be made clear when one farmer had from the other a statement in writing that he had purchased statutory seed.

Suppose I buy seed by sample and it is said to be No. 1, or No. 2, or No. 3, I have obtained it under this Act because this is the only Act that describes what No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3 seed is. I find afterwards that the seed contains noxious weeds. I fall back upon the dealer and ask damages from him because he gave me seed that was not up to the standard. Well, he would set up the plea that it was not sold under this Act, although as a matter of fact, it was sold under this Act for grade.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Agriculture proposes to amend section 0 by adding a subsection to be known as subsection (d) as follows :
Or to seed that, is grown and sold by any farmer on his own premises unless the purchaser of said seed demand's from the seller at the time of the sale thereof that the said seed he supplied to him subject to the provisions of this Act.
Suppose he buys it for No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3 it is subject to the provisions of this Act, and would he not be justified in setting up in court that it was bought under the provisions of this Act ?

1 think he could very well do that, but some proviso may be added to this subsection as the following which I merely suggest off-hand :	' which fact should be expressed in a receipt given for the payment for the seed.' The intention of this clause is that the purchaser shall ask a stipulation that the seed is sold to him under the provisions of this Act. That is a positive Act on the part of the purchaser and without that positive Act, on the part of the purchaser the idea is that the seller would not be subject to the provisions of the Act. Then, as a proof that the purchaser made that stipulation he should require it to be acknowledged in the receipt for the payment of the grain, and if it was not so acknowledged in the receipt for payment, then there would be no proof that he made such a stipulation. That would be proof in writing and that would be proof in writing
Hon.. Mr. FISHER.
which the purchaser would hold as he would his receipt for the payment.
You would make the seller give a certificate if the purchaser demanded it ?
Yes, and if the purchaser did not make that stipulation at the time of the transaction, then, the seller would be free from all responsibility under the provisions of this Act.
I am very much afraid that would be difficult to carry out.

I cannot see any difficulty in carrying out the intention of the hon. minister in connection with that matter. One farmer goes to another and says:
' I want to buy some seed.' The other asks:
' Do you want it for seeding purposes V 'Yes,' don't you know there is an Act governing the sale of grain for seed purposes ? Will you sell me seed that comes up to the requirements of the Act ?' 'Yes.' The bargain is made on that condition. 'Well' the purchaser says ' of course, you will give me a certificate to that effect'!' and the seller would say: 'Yes.' If the purchaser paid the seller .10 or 15 cents a bushel more for his grain because he required to use it for seed I should think he would have the right to get seed that would come under the provisions of the Act.

I would suggest to the hon. minister that it would be more practicable if he would insert the word 'obtains' in his amendment instead of the word * demands.' Otherwise we would be in this position that a farmer would say that he demanded a receipt but he would not have the benefit of getting it in writing. Unless lie had it in writing I do not think a case could be established. It is something like the law requiring the description of certain classes of merchandise to be in writing.
I refer to the statute of frauds. I do not think a person should be liable to the penalties of the Act unless it is conclusively shown that lie sold grain for seed purposes. The efficacy of the law would be taken away if there was no statement in writing, because the purchaser could come forward and say : It is true I got no writing. I have no evidence against this man in his own hand writing that he sold me this seed under tiiis Act; still, I am prepared to swear that I demanded it, and we would then be in the unfortunate position of having oath against oath. I think the hon. minister should put in the words ' unless he obtains,' because, if he does not obtain it he need not buy the seed. He should not buy the seed unless he obtains a receipt stating that the seed is sold under the provisions of the Act.
Mr. GILMOUR, Another way in which it could be made certain is by requiring that the farmer selling statutory seed should have tlie same mark on it that the merchant

is required to have who sells statutory seed. That would be proof positive.

The amendment as it stands, I think, perhaps, would be a little more perfect if the change which my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) suggests were made and if the word ' obtains ' were substituted for the word ' demands,' and a change were made providing that a certificate should be supplied to the purchaser stating that the seed supplied to him was subject to the provisions of this Act. I propose that the amendment shall read as follows :
(a.) Or to seed that is grown and sold by any farmer on his own premises, unless the purchaser of siaid .seed obtains from the seller at the time of the sale thereof a certificate that the said seed be supplied to him subject to the provisions of this Act.
Amendment agreed to.

My hon. friend from Ontario (Mr. Ross) asked on a previous occasion as to the effect of section (b) of clause 6, which, as printed, reads :
Any person selling seeds direct to merchants to be cleaned and graded before being offered for sale for the purposes of seeding.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ross) suggested that this would not protect the farmer who sold to a country merchant who did not intend to grade or clean the seed, but to sell it again to a regular seed dealer who had an appliance for cleaning and grading; I have consulted several lawyers, and especially the deputy of my department, and they hold that the words ' to be cleaned and graded before being offered for sale ' relieve the farmer from any responsibility who sells to the country merchant, who in turn sells to the larger merchant, with the intention of having the seed cleaned and graded before being sold for seeding purposes. The belief is that this clause completely protects the country merchant who purchases from the farmer with the intention afterwards of selling to the seed merchant, who would clean and grade.

I buy a great many seeds, and some that are not sold by retail or sold for seeding. We handle a great many seeds which are sold to dealers, who, in their turn, reclean and grade them, and under these circumstances, I was anxious to know whether I could still continue my business.. I am glad to hear from the hon. minister that the clause covers that. I would suggest to him that the word ' or ' should be substituted for the word ' and,' so that the clause would read :
Any person selling seeds direct to merchants to be cleaned * or ' graded.
We avoid as much as possible buying uncleaned small seed, that is seed that has the chaff in it, just as it comes from the thresh-227
ers, but sometimes we are compelled to take it. We also buy seed which the farmer calls sufficiently clean, and if the word ' or ' were inserted, that seed could be sold for grading purposes. It perhaps might not be quite clean, but it would go to be graded and if the word ' or ' were inserted, it would cover that. I think it would improve the section.

Some seedsmen in my locality buy seeds from the farmers and sell them wholesale or retail, but never clean them, because they have no cleaning apparatus. Suppose they sold to a person who did not clean or grade it, what would be the condition then ?
If the farmer sold it for seeding purposes, the farmer would be liable.
But the farmer might say that he did not sell it for seeding purposes.

The merchant who sold it to another farmer for seeding purposes would be liable. If the country nferchant sold it to a seed merchant who went into |the cleaning and grading of seeds, the country merchant would not be liable, because he is selling it for the purpose of cleaning and grading, and not for seeding. I do not think there is any objection to the word ' or ' being substituted for the word ' and,' and perhaps it may improve the section. This clause would not cover the case where the country merchant sold uncleaned seed to a farmer for seeding purposes, and I do not think it ought, because the country merchant should be subject to the same law as the wholesale seed dealer if he sells to a farmer for seeding purposes.

I am told by a gentleman of experience that this law would drive a number of men out of the business, and therefore it would reduce the competition in the sale of seed. I gave this Bill to a gentleman to examine it carefully, and he said that either the Act must remain a dead letter or otherwise a number of persons who dealt in seed would be liable to be mulcted very frequently. This gentleman has handled seeds for the last twenty years, and he has no apparatus for cleaning them. Another gentleman who does purchase and clean seeds told me that he thought he would not be able to carry on his business under this Bill, It seems to me that the measure is likely to be very unpopular. It might be made as perfect as possible, and then allow it to stand over for another session, until we get suggestions from seedsmen and farmers which would make it workable.

That is what we are trying to do now. There is no doubt that the country merchants who sell seeds to the farmers for seeding purposes ought to be liable to the same conditions as the general seed merchants.

If a merchant takes so little interest in his business that he would not prepare himself to clean the seed and make it fit for farmers to use, he should not be allowed to stay in the business to the detriment of all the farmers who dealt with him.
Mr. HcuHES (P.E.I.). If this Bill does not prevent men from selling the seeds of noxious weeds for good seeds, then it is of no use at all. If you make the Bill so that it will allow a man to sell weed seeds for other seeds, and if he can go on with his business in that line just as before, then there would be no use placing this Act upon the statute-book. My hon. friend seems to wish to make the Bill so wide and easy in order to make it workable, that it will work no injury to any man, and he can sell what he likes. Certainly the Bill must interfere with the business of those men who sell noxious weed seeds, no matter who they may be, and every person recognizes that a great deal of harm is done in that way. We recognize that by passing this Bill, and I would suggest that this clause be allowed to go through as it is.

I am simply drawing attention to the objection which has been raised by the men in the business. These men very often purchase from one farmer and sell to another. They do that for the convenience of the farmers, and no doubt make a little profit out of the transaction as well. It is because of the contention of these men that they cannot carry on their business without violating the law, that I am suggesting that we should not pass the Bill at once, but let it stand over in order to see if some suggestion cannot be made whereby these men shall be able to carry on their business, and do it profitably without violating the law.

There is no doubt that this Bill is a very serious matter, both to the seedsman and to the farmer. We are not likely to place ourselves in danger of coming under the penalties of this Act without taking the greatest precaution in regard to the seeds we buy. The farmers who produce the seeds have not yet had an opportunity to make careful preparation for the Act. When the farmer has had an opportunity to learn that he cannot sell the poor-seed which he has been in the habit of producing, he will not produce It. If this measure be made law now, he not only looses the value of his hay crop, but his seed as well. It would be a very serious mistake to bring this Act into force at once. I notice from * Hansard ' that when the Bill was discussed last week, the hon. minister said that the farmers had not the necessary machinery for cleaning seed. I think every farmer who cleans seed for sale should have the necessary machinery. It Is a very simple thing. A farmer can Hon. Mr. FISHEfi.
get a perfect seed mill for $25, and that would enable him to sell his seed to his neighbour. Under existing conditions, as the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) stated the other night, it would be necessary to establish seed shops in every township. The farmers ought to have the machinery necessary to put their grain into marketable condition before they can sell it, and there is no reason why they should not have such machinery.

My hon. friend was not here the other evening when I stated the result of the tests made of various samples of seed; but they show that even without any warning such as that which has been before the country by reason of the discussion of this Bill, the proportion of seed which is bad in this way is not so very great
I do not see quite clearly how a farmer would know, when he is offering seed for sale, say to a jobber, whether it is to be re-cleaned or not. In what way is the farmer to be relieved?

In any prosecution under the Act, the proof would have to be brought forward. As a general rule, jobbers do not buy seed for seed purposes. In the case mentioned, the jobber would have to prove that he had bought it for seed purposes.
The farmer would have to ask the purchaser whether the seed was to be re-cleaned and graded or not ?

I do not think so. The clause does not mean that.
Section 6 agreed to.
On section 7,
Every person who, by himself or through the agency of another person, violates any of the provisions of sections 3, 4 and 5 of this Act, shall, on summary conviction, be liable to a fine for the first offence not exceeding twenty-five dollars and not less than five dollars, and for each subsequent offence not exceeding fifty dollars and not less than ten dollars, together with the costs of prosecution, for each receptacle, package, sack or bag in or from which seeds are sold, offered, exposed or had in possession for sale, contrary to the provisions of the said sections ; and, in default of paying such fine and costs, shall be liable to imprisonment. with or without hard labour, for a term not exceeding one month, unless such fine and the costs of enforcing it are sooner paid.

I understand that the penalties imposed by this Act are taken from the Adulteration Act. There is no Charge that either the seedsmen or the farmers of the country have been guilty of anything in the shape of adulteration, and I think the penalties are unnecessarily severe. I notice that the amendment of

the minister has reduced them considerably-but I think they should be made simply nominal, for the purpose of carrying out the Act as intended. I understand perfectly well that the minister has no intention of doing an injustice to the farmer or any injury to the seedsman; blit that his object is only to make them both live up as closely to this Act as possible.

I do not think the penalties imposed in this section are at all undue.
On section 7a,
Any person domiciled within the Dominion ot Canada who sells seeds in packages, sacks or bags, sealed by him, shall alone be held to the observance of the provisions of this Act with respect to said seeds, so long as the same are sold without the seal thereon being broken ; and such person shall not be responsible therefor after the seal thereon is broken, unless at the time of breaking of said seal a sample of said seeds for official test is taken and inclosed in a sealed (package in the presence of two noninterested witnesses ; and in no case shall the responsibility of such person for such seeds extend beyond ninety days from the date cf placing the seal thereon, which date must be plainly marked on said packages, sacks or bags.
How will that affect the retail merchant who gets long grass or clover in seed packages of a quarter of a pound each? There is no seal on them, but they are just fastened together with mucilage.
A seal would have to be put upon the package. The wholesale dealer is only held responsible so long as the seal is unbroken.
The time limit is ninety days. Suppose the seedsmen did not dispose of the seeds inside that time ?
He could no longer hold the wholesale dealer responsible, unless before the ninety days he had taken a sample and inclosed it in a sealed package.
Every package should show on its face the date on which it was put up.
The clause says so.
In what position would the seller be after ninety days ?
He then would be responsible.
Does the hon. minister intend appointing an inspector ?
I have no intention of appointing an inspector outside the present staff of the department.

After ninety days that wholesale dealer is not responsible ? He
227i
must put a date on each seal. But he may be putting up and sealing thousands of these packages, must he stamp them all ?
Is it the date of the sale or the shipment that he puts on the seal ? Suppose a sale was made in July for shipment in October, which date would be put on ?

I should suppose myself that the seal would be put on at the time the seeds were put up. Of course the wholesaler might chose to put up a lot of packages before making a sale. In such a case, he would put a date on each. If the seeds are sealed up for ninety days, they would be as likely to deteriorate in the hands of the wholesaler as*the retailer.
Suppose the wholesaler puts up impure seeds and keeps them in his store until the ninety days have expired and then sells them, is he relieved from responsibility ?
Yes, he is after the ninety days.
A wholesale dealer has a lot of seed. He puts up a portion of it at the beginning of the ninety days and the rest of the stuff he does not put up until after the ninety days-what is the object ?

The seed merchants complain that they might put up perfectly pure seed which would go into the hands of the retailer, and then the retailer would adulterate the seed, but the name of the wholesale dealer would be on the package. A farmer who bought from the retailer a package, might sample and test it, and find that the seed was adulterated and he would come on the retail dealer. But the retail dealer would say : I bought that from the wholesale dealer as pure seed, and I ought not be liable. The wholesale dealer, whose name is on the package, wants protection, and we are providing protection, if he chooses to put a seal on the package which he sells to the retailer. As long as that seal is unbroken, he is held responsible during ninety days from the date of putting on the seal. As soon as the seal is broken or the ninety days have expired, he is no longer responsible.
When do the ninety days begin to count ?

From the time the seal is put on. The retailer can protect himself, when he opens the package, by taking out a sample and by inclosing it under seal in another package in the presence of two witnesses.
Suppose the retailer opens the bag and sells part of it, what becomes of the rest ?

The retailer is responsible after the seal

7209
is broken. But if be keeps tbe seal over' ninety days without breaking tbe seal, tbe wholesaler will be no longer responsible.
May not tbe retailer then sell that seed ?.
Yes, but subject to tbe provisions of tbe Bill. If he sells seed mixed with weeds or which does not germinate, be will be liable to tbe penalty.

Does tbe bon. minister mean to say that if a wholesaler sells a retailer seeds on a ninety day guarantee, that guarantee does not start at tbe time tbe goods are shipped ? If it starts sixty days before tbe goods are shipped, then tbe retailer has only thirty days in which to recoup himself.

Tbe wholesaler is relieved of tbe responsibility after tbe seal is broken or after ninety days. If the retailer thinks that tbe date of tbe seal is too far back, be need not purchase it, or be may insist, that tbe seal be dated when be purchases the seed.
Has be that privilege ?

Certainly. The only thing is, tbe wholesaler is responsible so long as bis seal is unbroken, up to a limit of ninety days. If the seal is broken, tbe retailer has to assume the responsibility, except that be takes a sample of the seed and that sample will be proof of tbe quality. If tbe retailer, however, bolds tbe seed for longer than ninety days be is responsible, no matter whether tbe seal is broken or not.
Does tbe bon. minister intend keeping a check on this sealing up business? Is he going to have an inspector in every seed warehouse in Canada ?

This is simply a matter of precaution as between the wholesaler and tbe retailer. Tbe wholesaler is afraid the retailer will change the seed in tbe packages. Suppose, for instance Mr. Rennie, of Toronto, should sell seed to John Jones, a country merchant. He puts on the package his name, ' Rennie,' a name which carries weight in the seed market. The retailer takes the seed out of the package and fills the package with other seed, selling it as Rennie's. If the retailer were fined for selling such seed, Mr. Rennie's reputation would suffer.
And so would that of the retailer.
But he would try to evade the blame by saying that he had: received the seed from Rennie and was faultless in the matter.
Was there ever a case in which a retailer was fined for selling impure seeds ?

There has been no law under which he could be fined, except_the common law. We are trying to provide machinery to meet such cases. The seed merchants tell us that if the Bill had not such provision they might be liable to such misrepresentation and they wish to be protected. This clause is for the purpose of providing means by which a wholesale seed merchant may protect himself in a certain manner for a certain time.
But suppose a retailer bought a thousand packages of seed. If he wished to protect himself must he take a sample of every half-pound package ?
As a matter of fact, seed merchants do not sell seeds in packages, except garden flower seeds, which are to be exempt from the operation of this law.
Turnip and carrot seeds are sold in packages.
As between the wholesaler and the retailer, they are sold in bulk, and the retailer puts them in smaller packages.

I beg'the kon. gentleman's pardon-these seeds are sold by the wholesaler in packages. We buy nearly all our mangel seeds in packages, because they are supposed to be a little better. And the same way with turnip seeds.
Such transactions will not come within the operation of the Act when the word ' vegetable ' is struck out of the third section.

There is one point I would like to understand. A wholesale! sells seeds in sealed packages. At the end of ninety days he is relieved of responsibility. But suppose after ninety days the package is broken open and it is found to contain a large proportion of weed seeds. Is the wholesaler responsible or is he still relieved of responsibility ?
The retailer would be responsible and the wholesaler would be relieved.
I do not think the law should be made to work that way.
That is the effect of the Bill.

The whole thing is a little seedy.
