speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We were considering clause 7a.
It seems to me that clause is hardly what it ought to he to protect the retail dealer. While it would he a protection to the wholesale man, it would be little protection to the retailer.

Perhaps the date ought to be reckoned from the sale of the seeds. In that adjoining -section, I had intended that the sealing should be done at the time of the sale or the shipment. I had no idea of seed being put up in quantities with the seal on it -while still held in the hands of the dealer for future sale. If that were done, it would to a certain extent meet the in-tion of the section. I would therefore be disposed to change the section and make it read :
In no ease shall the responsibility of such person for such seeds extend beyond ninety days friom the date of the sale thereof.
Instead of saying 'the date of placing the seal thereof.'
That is better.

That might be still a little indefinite; the sale and the shipment might not necessarily be at the same time. Now, the sale might be held to take place at the time the order was given, though the dealer might not deliver for several months after, in which case ninety days ought to be counted from the time he put up the seeds and shipped them. I would ask the opinion of the bon. member for Hamilton, who is in the trade.
Do I understand this refers to clover and grass seeds?
Yes.
Exclusively?
To all seeds that come under the operation of the Act.

It would be rather a serious matter for the dealers. Clover and grass seed are sold entirely for cash, we draw immediately upon shipment. If the buyer were enablej to hold this seed for ninety deys and then to put in a complaint about it, it would be a very serious obstacle to the business. The profits on clovers and grass seeds are infinitesimal, and the dealers could not afford to carry the seeds for a long time. If it was simply a matter of forty or fifty bags of seed, the country dealer could test the seed without breaking the seal, except of one bag, and make a complaint if necessary. He could try a bag of seed with one of these little triers as soon as he received it, and if he had any objection he could make a complaint to the shipper. But no seedsman could possibly
do business under that provision and carry it for ninety days.

I have proposed another section 12 instead of the present section 12, which will read :
Amy sample of seeds taken from any seeds which are found or suspected to be sold in violation of tihe provisions of this Act, shall, within a delay of seven days, be reckoned (a) in the oase of seeds under seal as aforesaid, from the date of the breaking of the seal ; in all other cases, from the date on which the said seed entered into the personal possession and became the property of the purchaser.
The printed section 12 says simply seven days in all cases, it was Intended to he seven days after breaking the seal. Of course, in that case the test need not be made at any time during the ninety days, or until breaking the seal.

Seven days after breaking the seal would not answer tlie purpose, because be might carry it for the full ninety days and be would still be under obligation. I think the seven days given to the wholesaler after shipment would be quite sufficient for a cash article, when settlement is to be made immediately upon receipt of the seed.

During seven days the seal should not be broken, because the moment the seal is broken and the bag opened, the wholesale man should not he held responsible for that opened hag, because other seed might be put into it.

The intention is that the wholesaler shall only be responsible until the seal is broken. The ninety days is rather a restriction of that, because even if the seal was not broken at the end of ninety days, the wholesaler would be relieved of all responsibility.

I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton. Why should the wholesaler have ninety days ? He can ascertain directly whether it is up to the standard or not, and he should he relieved at once. To carry it for ninety days would almost mean that the money should not be paid until the ninety days were over.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would like the minister to explain how the penalties imposed by this Act will be enforced when a conviction is secured against either the wholesale merchant or the retail merchant. Is it expected that every retail merchant will be an analyst, and that be will know when he opens the bag whether the seed comes up to tlie standard or not ?
He will take a sample and send it to the analyst in the department, who will test it for him and report.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But before be gets that done tbe season will be over for making use of tbe seed.

As I understand it, tbe department will regulate the grades of the seed at tbe beginning of tbe season, so that not only tbe wholesale seedsman but the retailer will understand what tbe grades are. If tbe wholesale seedsman ships to tbe retailer, tbe latter can get samples from the department here ncccord-ing to the grades they have established, 1, 2 or 3, and be can compare tbe shipment with tbe sample from tbe department. It would be a simple matter, on the receipt of any shipment, to tell whether tbe seed is up to grade. But there should be no indefinite time such as ninety days, because it would be impossible to conduct business under those conditions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That may be the plan by which the minister intends to work it out for the security of the retail merchant. But I am bound to say that there is not a retail merchant in the country who is competent to discover from a sample of timothy seed how many foul seeds there may be in it. I could tell d^iisy seed in a sample of timothy, but there are other foul seeds more injurious than daisy that I could not tell. Let me give an illustration : A retail merchant sends to my hon. friend, or to Mr. Rennie, the seedsman whom the minister recommended, for a bag of timothy or of clover or of alsike. He receives these three bags stamped with the name of the seed merchant and there is a seal on them. He breaks the seal before he can look at the seed. The seedsman is liberated as soon as the seal is broken. The dealer breaks the seal in the presence of two farmers. The seed looks all right at the mouths of the bags. It may be up to the standard so far as he is competent to judge. He takes a sample out of each bag in the presence of the farmers, they seal . the samples up, put their names upon them and they are put away in a drawer. Then the merchant deals out to the first farmer a peck or a bushel taken from each of these bags. The other farmer wants the same quantity and he gets his peck or bushel out of each of these bags. Then the farmers go home to their farms. They have both clean land on which to sow the seed. After they have sown their grain they sow their timothy and their alsike. It will not develop foul seed at once. When the farmer cuts bis crop of grain off he finds that he has a good catch of seed, but it does not fully develop until next spring, and then he gets his crop of hay. Perhaps one of those farmers will say that the seed produced its kind and that he never had better seed on the farm. The other will come back to tbe merchant and say : The crop the seed for which I got from you, was full of foul weeds. How is the hon.
minister going to convict the merchant who sold the seed ?
A sample is taken and either of these farmers who bought the seed can have that sample forwarded to the seed laboratory and a test will show the exact condition of the seed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I explained that the sample was taken, but it was from the mouth of the bag. One farmer had got his seed out of the mouth of the bag while the foul seed was found below that.
A proper sample would not be taken out of the mouth of the bag.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is he going to empty that bag out in order to get a sample ?

No, there is a very simple contrivance costing about twenty-five cents by which they can take samples from any portion of the bag. A proper sample would be taken in that way.
Mr. TAYLOIi. Then, each merchant who handles seed has to provide himself with one of these contrivances ?

I think it will be wise for him to do so.
Mr. TAYLOR, If you establish a laboratory and the sample upon examination is found to be foul, perhaps the farmer could get back at the wholesale merchant, but the farmer cannot tell for six or eight months after he has sown the seed whether he has foul seed or not. It would be impossible for him to prove that he purchased this foul seed from the merchant because any man might walk upon the farm at night and sow foul seed. It looks as if this Bill will be entirely unworkable, a great disturbance to the trade and of no great benefit to the country.

My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is perfectly right in saying that somebody could walk upon a farmer's land and sow foul seed, although I do not think it is at all likely to be done by any person but the farmer himself, but I admit frankly that the growth of weeds is not a sufficient proof that the seed contained foul weed seeds. Many weed seeds will stay for a considerable length of time in the land before germinating and they are carried by wind and birds from one farm to another, and from one field to another, but, I think the machinery that we propose is quite sufficient to prove the quality of the seed that is sown. That is all we can do. We do not expect to perform miracles, but we believe that we can minimize the risks and difficulties attendent upon the sale of seed.

Section 3 says that any person who sells seeds containing noxious weed seeds shall be liable. It is not the intention of the hon. minister to allow either the 90 day or the 7 day clause to interfere with that prohibition as far as noxious weeds are concerned, is it ? I presume that must refer to germination.

The seven days is merely the time within which the sample must be taken. This is simply to insure that the sample by which the shipment or delivery of seeds is judged shall be taken at once. If it is not taken at once it would not be fair to judge the seeds by that sample. The seven days period is given as a reasonable time within which the merchant can take his sample. I think there might be a less delay than that-three or four days possibly. The 90 days in clause 7 deals with a totally different point, and I am not at all certain from what has fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Bruce) but what it would be better to expunge that part from the guarantee. I can understand from what he says the difficulties in the trade which might arise from the insertion of the 90 days clause. I would be disposed from what he says to leave that out. That was Simply put in as an assistance to the wholesale dealer to limit his responsibility. Even if the seal was unbroken he should not be responsible for more than 90 days, but if that is stricken out, then he would be responsible just.as long as the seal was unbroken.

This thing will gradually rectify itself. When this law passes and the seed dealers find it is necessary for them to have clean seed, they will send an inspector around themselves and see where the grain is being grown and that there are no weeds in it. For example, we grew a large quantity of pease for sale to the American market, and we hand-picked them- all, and have fifty or sixty women picking them over, so that they would be perfectly clean. The American purchasers of these seeds sent out inspectors, who went through the fields where the pease were grown, and if they found there were any weeds in the crop they would have them picked out. The seedsmen who will buy these seeds will similarly go to the farmer and see whether the fields are perfectly clean or not.

I appreciate very highly the statement of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Bruce) with regard to the educational work that has been done in the country by the officers of my department. I am glad to hear that the people are asking for the best quality of seeds, and that is a most gratifying fact to me as the result of work which has been done by my department. I believe that that educational work will go on in the future as it has been going on in the past. The hon. gentleman says that if this Act was to come into force lie would reject about 50 per cent of the seed which he purchases from the farmers, instead of 10 per cent as now. That would be one of the most beneficial educational forces that could be exerted in the country. Mv hon. friend (Mr. Bruce) and some others of the most reliable and most experienced dealers in the country do reject seed which is full of impurities when it comes into them, and if they would reject more I am satisfied that it would be all the better. Some may say that this is going to cut some

farmers out of their seed trade, but if it is going to cut the farmers out of the sale of weed seeds, I would be glad of it. That action on the part of the seed dealers will accomplish much in an educative way. It is not so long since country store keepers purchased good, bad and indifferent butter, and paid an average price per pound for it, but that kind of thing has passed away in this country, and to-day the farmer who makes good butter gets a better price for it than the farmer who makes bad butter. And so if the seed merchants will pay the farmers according to the quality of the seed, the farmer will soon find that it will pay him better to keep his seeds cipan. If the seed merchants would go a little further and, as my hon. friend from Renfrew lias described, send inspectors out to examine the fields, they will get better seeds than they now do. It may be that some of them do it now, but, judging by this discussion, I do not think that they engage in such work as this.
'Seven out of ten farmers sell more or less seed every year, and that would practically mean that you would have to inspect every farm.

I think the seed merchants, as a rule, buy from particular farmers, and they could examine the fields of these farmers without much trouble. In the case cited by the member for Renfrew, the inspectors were sent to Canada by the United States seed merchants.

In my section of the country men will come in with a load of seed fifteen or twenty miles, and that seed will include alsike, mammoth clover and different others, and if you followed out that plan, you might as well go out and inspect every farm.
Do I understand that the minister expects the seedsmen to inspect the fields ?
I did not say I expected it, but I think in many instances it would be advisable.

Many of the best farmers make a practice of going over the fields before they are cut, because if there are weeds in the field it is utterly impossible to separate the weed from the seed when the threshing takes place. A careful farmer will cut the weeds before the crop is cut.
I wish to address some observations to the minister in regard to the question of germination. I think the seedsmen who interviewed the Minister of Agriculture mentioned that it would be very difficult for them to comply with the regulations with regard to germination. For instance, I get a carload of seed to-day and I ship out the most_ of it that day or the following day, and it is impossible for me to test the ger-Hon. Mr. FISHER.
urination in that time. With a short season, lasting three or four months, and carloads going out and carloads coming in, it would be impossible to test tlje germination. I know perfectly well that there is very little difficulty with regard to timothy and clover, because, if you get new seeds and you can tell them by their colour, there is never any doubt about the germination, so that we pay very little attention to the question of germination in clover and timothy. In the case of vegetables and feed seeds, we are most particular. We get them in bulk from growers early in the season, and we have an opportunity to test their germinating qualities long before they are sold. It would be utterly impossible for us to test the germination of clover and grasses as they come in and go out ; but, of course, we can tell very easily whether they are new or old seeds. It does not pay any dealer to carry seeds over for one year. The interest on the seeds carried over will amount to the profit.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the minister to say, before recess, that the ninety-day limit he thought quite sufficient, because during those ninety days the seeds would deteriorate, particularly timothy. Now, I would like to ask my hon. friend from Hamilton, who is a practical man, will timothy seed deteriorate in ninety days ?
Not unless it happens to be mouldy or heated. If it is in perfect condition when put into the bags, it will keep for three years.
The hon. gentleman misquoted me. I said timothy seed which had lost its hulls. I think that makes a difference.

Hulled timothy seed will retain its vitality for three years, and I do not think you will find any difference in its germination.
The MINISTER | OF AGRm Ll LTURE. I think, from what I have been told, that a seed expert as a rule can tell pretty well the germinating quality of a seed by looking at it-not absolutely perhaps, but pretty closely ; and I think I am justified in saying that from what my hon. friend has just said.
There is no doubt about that at all. We would not be afraid of the restrictions of the Act in reference to germination.

The germinating quality of good, healthy, fresh clover and grass seed is usually all right. But the seeds with which the farmers with us find the greatest trouble are mangold seeds and beet seeds. It is the very common opinion among farmers that the dealers, when they keep the seeds over a year, steep the old seeds, skim off those that float, and mix the others with the new seeds and sell them. There is a great complaint in our part of

the country that not one-half or one-quarter of the mangold or beet seeds will grow. We scarcely ever hear a complaint about clover or grass seed.
Do I understand that that method, of putting seeds in water, is taken with seeds not immediately planted ?
It is said so. I do not know whether it is true or not.
I would' not think that seeds put into water to be tested in that way would afterwards be sold as a commercial article.

I would say, in reply to the hon. member for East Grey, that the idea that old seeds are put into water so that the defective seed may be floated or skimmed oft is an absolute fallacy. It would be impossible to turn over tons of stuff to swim it, and then dry it again. I never heard of such a thing being done. With regard to the germination of mangold or sugar beet seeds, I may say that every perfect seed will produce a true plant, and mangold seeds will retain their vitality for a long time ; but no seedsman or grower can take the responsibility of making a seed germinate after it is put in the ground, if it has not the proper conditions of soil, climate and rain.

But where the conditions seem to be favourable in every respect, the soil properly worked up and the moisture all right, you naturally look for a fair proportion of the seeds to grow ; but when you find that only one-half or one-quarter of them grow, you naturally conclude that the seed could not have been very good.
I will ask that the section immediately after section 7a be allowed to stand for further consideration, as it is not in quite the shape in which it ought to be for an enactment.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister had better let the whole Bill stand. As it is to-day, with all the amendments made to it, the hon. gentleman would hardly recognize it as his own child. It came before the House in such a crude shape that it required all these amendments. I think he had better take the advice of his friends on both sides and ask that the committee rise, report progress and sit again next session.

There are some other things to be considered before we reach that point.
Section allowed to stand.
Off section 8,

The purchaser might not be a bona fide purchaser. He might just have bought a pound of seed to put himself within the law and become a common informer. There is nothing worse in our country than the trade of the informer. It is most disreputable and leads to serious consequences. We had a sample of it in the working out of the Scott Act, and this would not be mush better. The amendment which the hon. minister has proposed does not improve his Bill.

I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend from Middlesex. Whatever may he the penalty, and it should not be too large-it ought to go entirely to the government. We ought not to encourage people to become informants because there are too many men looking after such opportunities. I do not think that our seedsmen and farmers should be brought into the category of misdemeanants.

I do not think that the dangers alluded to need be apprehended. Reference has been made to the Scott Act. Well, my own county was under that Act many years, and we had no abuses such as those mentioned. I know that in some parts of the country it was said that such abuses took place, but I think the reports were exaggerated. It was a very rare occurrence indeed when anybody gave information simply to get the fee. The reason for this clause is that the farmer or purchaser of seed, who has suffered by reason of his having purchased improper seed, is performing a public service when he prosecutes the seller; but if he has to do it at his own expense, he will probably think that he has suffered enough already, without going to the trouble of a prosecution, when he has to run all the risk without any chance of being reimbursed. However, I am in the hands of the committee and quite content to abide by its decision.

This kind of legislation is not right. If a farmer is aggrieved he has his remedy. He can bring an action and have the man fined. In my opinion the whole money should go to the Crown. A very special case would have to be made out before I would consent to furnishing opportunities to our farmers to go into the

business of informing. I would ask the hon. minister to strike out that clause.

As the sense of the committee is against the clause, I withdraw my motion.
Motion withdrawn.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE moved that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I would suggest to the hon. minister that he should have this Bill reprinted so that we may see exactly what it is. It has met with considerable opposition, but I believe that there is more merit in it than there was in the Fruits Marks Act, because in that Act the packers of apples are required to be learned in the law. They have to bring out the statute and lay it on the barrel in order to mark their barrels in accordance with the statutes. Then should they mark their barrels wrong-and they might easily do that because the quality of the fruit is only a matter of opinion-they are responsible for their action. This Bill has more merit than even the Butter Bill, because that Bill gave a privilege to certain individuals to stamp their butter as creamery butter which was refused to the other individuals just as well entitled to it. And in another part of that Bill, dairy butter of the commonest quality is allowed to be freely sold, but you are not allowed to clarify it and sell it after it has been thus made more palatable. I hope that the hon. minister will be able to make this Bill workable, as in such case it will be better perhaps for the country.

I am exceedingly gratified by the compliment which my hon. friend has paid me when he said that there is more merit in this Bill than in the Fruits Marks' Act. That Act has done inestimable good to the fruit trade. Of this I have convincing proofs every day, not only in this country but in Europe. In saying therefore that this measure has more merit than the Fruits Marks' Act, he is paying it the highest possible compliment.

I would like to ask another question. Should this Bill become law, suppose a farmer finds seeds, which were sold to him as pure, to be mixed with obnoxious weeds, would he not have an action for damage against the seedsman, even though the seedsman stated in his catalogue that he did not guarantee the seed. The seedsman could not shelter himself behind this Act. The law makes the standard. The standard says the seed shall be pure, and the farmer purchases it, believing it to be pure. Suppose he finds it is not pure, what remedy would the farmer have in law against the seller ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) ought not to ap-Mr. ROSS .(Ontario).
peal to) me on a question of law for I am not a lawyer-
But the hon. gentleman has the Minister of Justice beside him.

But, without appealing to the Minister of Justice, and even though I am not a lawyer, there are one or two things in the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Sproule) remarks which I think I can answer. There is nothing in this Act to prevent an action under the civil law for damages. This Act is of the nature of a criminal law and provides for penalties.
And not damages for loss sustained ?

No, that is a matter of civil rights, and, as such, I understand, comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures- I am speaking subject to correction as a layman. But this Bill would not prevent one from obtaining damages for an injury done.
It would strengthen his case immensely.
To provide something of that kind ? But it would be ultra vires of this parliament.

The hon. minister misunderstands me. If a man purchases seeds under this Act, they must conform to a certain standard. And if the seller were condemned under this law for selling impure seed, that fact would immensely strengthen the case of the complainant going into court claiming damages.
Which is an argument for the passing of this Act.
I am not objecting to it, but rather commending that feature of it.

I appreciate that, and I think the hon. gentleman is right. This will provide machinery by which a man could sustain an action for damages better than could be done at the present time. The members of the committee have discussed this Bill pretty generally. Before the committee rises, I would like to say that I think I have accomplished what I had hoped for in the discussion. I have had the advantage of the opinion of the members of the House which I asked for when I first introduced the Bill in committee. I am sure that these opinions and the discussion which has arisen here will assist very much in the perfecting of this law. If its passage is delayed for another year, the discussions which have taken place this session will not be lost by any means. I trust that as a consequence of the discussion the people who are interested in the seed trade, the farmers who purchase, the men who handle and the deal-

ers who grade the seeds, will study the proposed law, and will give us the benefit of that study. And I trust that, as a result of all1 this the law will be more perfect than it could otherwise have been made on a first attempt at legislation of this kind.
Will the hon. minister have the Bill printed as he intends to have it enforced at a future date ?
I will take steps to have the Bill printed as it is now before the committee.

I desire to thank the hon. Minister of Agriculture for the painstaking and careful way in which he has listened to every suggestion that has been offered. But I trust he will see the absurdity of the suggestion of the hon. member for Grey that he should follow up a dealer who has sold a lot of timothy or clover and allow the buyer to come back for damages against the seedsmen because there might possibly be mustard in the seeds he bought. The buyer has an opportunity to see the seed and know whether their is a mustard in it, for the mustard seeds can be detected at once; moreover, no seedsman who knows his business will sell clover with mustard in it. because the mustard can easily be seen and easily removed. It may be that a crop of mustard will be found in land on which the seed is sown, but then the mustard may have been there for years, and it would be most unfair to subject the seedsman to a charge for that with which he had nothing to do.
Bill reported.

Mr. Spteaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to draw the attention of the House to the handsome trophy which stands on the Table. This is a trophy presented by the first battalion of the Gordon Highlanders to the Dominion Rifle Association, in commemoration of the services of the Canadian troops, especially of the first Royal Canadian regiment, in South Africa where they were the comrade regiment of the first battalion of the Gordon Highlanders. It is unnecessary for me to recount the glorious deeds of that historic regiment. This trophy is presented as a token of the friendship and comradeship existing between the regiments and that we trust will always last between the soldiers and citizens of Canada and the soldiers and citizens of the motherland.

Since my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) has referred
to the matter, perhaps I ought to say a word, as I am responsible for the trophy being placed in the position in which it is. A memorandum will be found immediately in front of the trophy which explains the source from which it came and the reason why it was sent here. I thought it would be agreeable for the members of the House to see it and to have this assurance of the high appreciation by that very gallant and distinguished regiment, the Gordon Highlanders, of the Canadian volunteers who served in South Africa. A tribute to our Canadian soldiers could not come from any higher source than from this gallant regiment with whom our men served side by side in the late war. I think it is a very great compliment to have been paid to our militia, and I am sure the militia throughout the country will appreciate to the full the great honour which has been done them. These are the words engraved upon the trophy :
Trophy presented by the 1st battalion of the Gordon Highlanders to the Dominion Rifle Association in remembrance of the spirit of comradeship which existed between that corps and the Canadian troops in South Africa during the South African campaign.
I am sure I need not add a word to this. It speaks volumes of itself.

There is a decrease here of $8,200, from the fact that this year we do not require the vote we bad last year for erecting school buildings.
How many Indian schools are there ?
There are 31 day schools in British Columbia, to which we give $300 each and one to which we give $400.
Perhaps the minister could tell us when these schools were established, whether many of them were established lately; also, what salaries are paid to the principals of these schools?

I cannot tell my hon. friend the time when each school was established. I suppose that could be found in the records of the department. In the case of day schools, whenever evidence is brought forward that there is need of a school in any particular district, I look into the information furnished, and if I think the need is pressing, I allow for a salary. The ordinary salary is $300. Most of these schools, in fact all the day schools, are carried on under the supervision of some religious body.
What kind of a school have you at Brandon ?

I would remind my hon. friend that. this item refers to the schools in British Columbia. I may answer, however, that the industrial school at Brandon was established about 1892 or 1893. The buildings were put up at that time.
On what principle do you supply medical attendance and medicines 7

We have practically the same arrangement there that we have in other places; we simply have to furnish medical attendance and medicines to the Indians where we find they are unable to do it for themselves, and we try to keep the expenditure down as low as possible. In British Columbia the expenditure on these items is increasing, and a considerable supplementary vote will be asked for during the present session for the coming year. It seems to be a fact that as the cai-e of the Indians in British Columbia has increased, the demands for medicines and medical attendance have also Increased. I suppose that is due to the fact that in former years, when less attention was paid to them, they did not make so many demands for medicines and medical attendance. Our experience is that as the province of British Columbia opens up and the Indians become better known to the agents and the people the demands constantly increase. We have some sala-' ried officers and we have some who are not under salary.	When they are not
salaried we pay them by fees. We prefer to have them salaried because then we know what we have to provide for.
What do you usually pay for salaries on an agency or reserve 7

Under the Indian Act. The Indian Act makes it a criminal offence to sell liquor to Indians.
Yes, but for instance, a prosecution took place on Manitoulin Island.

We have a license law in Ontario which provides a certain fine for any one selling liquor to Indians, and there is a much heavier penalty than for selling liquor to white men. In the event of a prosecution taking place where liquor is sold to Indians would you prosecute under the License Act or the Dominion Indian Act.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
We prosecute in every case under the Indian Act of the Dominion, which makes it an offence to sell liquor to Indians.
Mr.	SPROULE.	That applies all over
the Dominion ?

Yes.

Where do you find a return of these convictions 7
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
I am informed that there is no list published in the report of the department, but if it is thought desirable that such a list should be published there is no trouble in the world in embodying it. Attention has not been called to it before. We have in all cases reports from the agents of the convictions which have taken place.
Then, these reports, I assume, for any year can be obtained from the department.
Yes.
May I ask the hon. minister to give us a statement of the number of Indians in British Columbia 7
According to the census there are about 25,000.
Would the hon. minister give us some information in respect to their farming operations 7 I notice that the government are supplying a considerable quantity of seeds, &c. ?

I cannot give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) very much information about the farming of the British Columbia Indians, because they do not follow farming to any considerable extent. We have not in British Colubmia the system of teaching agriculture to the same extent that we have it among the Indians of the North-west Territories and Manitoba. The Indians of British Columbia are a different class altogether. The greater number of them do not live upon land suitable for farming and do not care to follow farming anyway. A great many of them follow fishing. Many of them go out to labour. They go out when the fishing season is on, and agriculture has not been developed amongst those Indians in the same way as it has been amongst other Indians. Probably the hon. member for Vic-

toria (Mr. Earle) could give more information upon tliat subject than I can.
Might I ask the hon. minister to give the Indian population of British Columbia to-day as compared with what it was ten years ago ?

My information is that there is practically very little variation in the Indian population as far as the information of the department goes. Referring to what my hon. friend asked me a few minutes ago, I find in the records of the department from the British Columbia agencies that the total amount of farm products of all kinds in'oduced in the different reserves in the whole of British Columbia last year amounted to $278,173, the larger portion of which would be hay.
I did not hear any answer to the question as to the salaries totalling $20,440. To what officials are these salaries paid ? Are they departmental officials V

Mr-. THOMSON (North Grey). I notice that we pay for medical attendance $11,000 ; for day schools for educating the Indians we pay $9,700, and for travelling expenses $5,600. I think it most inconsistent that we should pay $5,600 for travelling expenses and $9,700 for schools.

I am sorry to say that the objection which my hon. friend takes will probably be removed, because our medical attendance is growing larger, and not because we desire it either. So far as salaries in British Columbia are concerned, it is quite impossible to improve the position. The province is of vast extent, the agencies are separated in most cases by considerable distances, and it is quite impossible to secure the services of agents competent to do the work at salaries substantially less than those which we are paying. My recollection is that the salaries are a trifle less now than when I took office, but there is substantially no increase anyway. The principal expenditure must necessarily be the salary of a good man on the reserve to look after the work. There is an inevitable increase in medical attendance.
I do not see that there is the least power in the department to reduce these expenses.
These expenditures remind me of the Barney Ricketts road jobs in Muskoka, where they paid $300 for overseeing and travelling expenses and put $50 on the road.
It is most extraordinary that you provide the munificent sum of $4,500 for relief to the Indians and $1,000 for seed, while you pay $5,000. for travelling expenses.
I wish to ask the minister if any progress has been made in the negotiations for the removal of the Songhees reserve ?

Some years ago, after a great deal of discussion and trouble, an arrangement was made whereby it would have been possible to remove the Songhees Indians from their reserve. I personally recognized what every one must recognize who has seen the Songhees reserve in the city of Victoria, that it is a source of regret that the reserve should remain where it is. My hon. friend (Mr. Earle) is aware that when I was negotiating with the Indians some years ago, the local government interposed a difficulty which was explained shortly afterwards in this House. Since that time no other definite arrangement has been arrived at. About a year ago I had a discussion with Mr. Eb-berts, then Attorney General of the province of British Columbia, and I reviewed the whole situation with him, and I told him that I was perfectly agreeable to carry out any reasonable arrangement that might be made. I said to him, and I think another member of the local government was present, I said to him : If you carry out in substance the arrangement which I suggested at that time, I am willing to do all I can to give it effect. It was then arranged that Mr. Vowell, the Indian superintendent at Victoria, and the representatives of the local government should try and get together and work out .some kind of an arrangement whereby this should be done. I had hoped at that time that that would have been done, and I rather think that the reason why nothing very substantial has been done lias been owing to political changes in British Columbia which have taken up the attention of the local government very much. I am quite prepared, and have been prex>ared since 1897, to carry out the arrangement on the general lines on which we were negotiating at that time, and which I think are the only lines on w-hich an arrangement can be made. I may remind my hon. friend (Mr. Earle) that the rock on which we split is this. I said : I am willing to undertake the burden of getting the Indians to move,

and I am willing to recognize, in a sense, your reversionary title to the reserve, but you will have to furnish a reserve in place of the one which they have in the city and which the Indians will be willing to accept. That the local government was willing to do, but they said : If the reserve in the city sells for more money than the reserve which we give in its place costs, then we want that money. I said : I cannot, as trustee for the Indians, hand that money over to you, but I will fund that money, and if you establish your title to the money then you can have it. I could not feel it my duty, as superintendent general, to hand over that money to the local government. My impression is that at the last negotiations I had with them they expressed their assent to the proposition, which I had made before, and that the money should be funded, if there was any balance, and dealt with according as the iaw might direct later on. I am perfectly willing to do that now if the local government can give their attention to it and transact their part of the business. I cannot say at the present time if the Indians are willing to go, but at the time I made the proposition they were willing. I am safe in saying that at the time Mr. McKenna and Mr. Rothweil were there, in the summer of 1897, the Indians would have gone, but I cannot say now whether they would or not.

As I understand it, the arrangement, as outlined by the minister, is What took place, but I think there was always the difficulty that the Indians would not move, and it remained for the Dominion government to inforce their removal, provided the other conditions were carried out.
I do not think there would have been any trouble about their going in 1897.
I notice in the papers since we have been in session that the provincial government had about secured a site suitable for them.
In the proposition I made in 1897 I undertook that the department here would see that they moved, and we were satisfied from the report of our officers that they would go at that time. *

There is an expenditure here of 8140,000, and in that expenditure there is an item of nearly $70,000 for industrial and boarding schools. I understood from the minister that the British Columbia Indians were engaged as fishermen and as labourers, and I would like to know what is taught in these industrial schools, for which we pay such a large sum of money. The minister said that they were principally under the charge of the different religious bodies. What kind of teaching do they give in these schools that produce fisher-Hon. Mr. FISHER.
men and labourers ? I have no doubt that you are teaching these children some industry, and I would like to know if the minister thinks he is justified in making this large expenditure on education with apparently such barren results ? Are they, when they leave school, turned adrift to go fishing with their fathers and mothers, or do they take to agriculture or to some trade ?

The general question of policy as to Indian education is a very large question. The system of education by industrial schools was inaugurated a good many years ago. I have gone into that question pretty fully on other occasions when the Indian estimates have been before the House. My view generally has been that the establishment of further industrial schools should not be encouraged; because I found, on investigation shortly after I took office, that it was extremely problematical whether the results of the industrial schools were commensurate with the size of the expenditure upon them. I found, for instance, that boys and girls were in some cases kept in industrial schools until they were twenty-three or twenty-four years of age, and some of the officers of the department were afraid to let them out. I issued an order that no person should remain in an industrial school after the age of eighteen, and -the pupils who were above that age were got from the schools as quickly as possible, and placed according to the best judgment of the different agents. My view was that the money would be far better expended in giving; the Indian children a reasonable amount of education and civilization in ways by which a much larger number would be reached, than by concentrating the expenditure upon an alleged industrial education of a few. Therefore I have followed the policy of encouraging the establishment of boarding schools rather than industrial schools. The experience of the department has been that it is very difficult to get a satisfactory attendance at day schools. The children go back to their parents' homes, which are generally not of a very elevated character; they are very irregular in their attendance, and it is very difficult to improve them; although we have a considerable number of day schools where the circumstances do not warrant the establishment of boarding schools. But the policy ive have been following in recent years has been to establish boarding schools where the children are kept a much shorter time than they are at the industrial schools, and where the benefits are spread over a much larger number. It would not do to begin the policy of abolishing industrial schools, which have been establishsed at large expense, and where staffs have been appointed and equipment provided. I would not take the responsibility of recommending that these schools be adandoned or dismantled; but I have taken the responsibility of say-

ing that X would not encourage the establishment of further industrial schools. The effect of Indian education, in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, has been excellent. It has made a distinct improvement in the general tone of the Indians. I am satisfied that my hon. friend would receive testimony from those who live in the neighbourhood of the reserves that there is a vast difference between the Indians of the North-west now and the Indians of the North-west twenty or twenty-five years ago. At the present time the Indians are a comparatively civilized lot of people. I do not know that there is anything special to be said in regard to the work in British Columbia, except this, that the Indians of British Columbia originally were a much more turbulent lot of Indians than those in other portions of the country, especially those towards Fort Simpson and other parts of the North-west coast; and the fact that they are now a comparatively orderly and civilized community is largely due to the establishment by missionaries of mission stations and the establishment of industrial and other schools among them. Some years ago I visited Fort Simpson, where I saw an Indian village which no person at a little distance would imagine to be an Indian village, because it had all the characteristics of a respectable village of white people. I visited one house where an Indian who fifteen or twenty years before would have been a savage, occupied a comfortable little cottage with a sitting room which was carpeted and furnished with an organ and with other evidences of civilization. At Metlakatla we have had a considerable expenditure from time to time; but the agent there has had a very large band of Indians to look after. There too, I think the civilization of the Indians has proceeded at a very rapid rate. While the Indians of the northern portion of British Columbia were originally as much more savage and turbulent race than the Indians of other portions of Canada, yet they have had this other characteristic, that when they have adopted the ways of civilization, they have become much more like white men than the Indians of other parts of the country. There is a distinct difference between the Indian of British Columbia and the Indian of the North-west Territories. The Indian of British Columbia will go into the pit and the field and work at day's labour, while it is impossible to get the Indian of the Northwest Territories to do that. Many of the Indians of British Columbia are very comfortably off, and their villages are quite prosperous. The impression I derived from a trip which I made to British Columbia some years ago was that there was no part of Canada where the expenditure of the government in assisting the different churches and in carrying on educational work among the Indians has been productive of more beneficial results.

I would like to ask the minister some further questions regarding travelling expenses, for which I think the amount charged is very large in proportion to the whole. In the Auditor General's Report for 1902, at page J

73, I find the following .

Viowell; board and lodging, $148.50 ; cabs and porters, $30 ; barbers and laundry, $2.65; ferriage and street cars, $4.70; fares, $101.90 ; pullmans, $39.75 ; livery and horse hire, $99 ; hire of launch, one day, $10.
I do not know whether this is some ambassador travelling in state, or an ordinary agent of the department; but from the expense account he sends in, he must be a man of considerable importance. $5,600 out of $137,000, is a large proportion for travelling expenses, and I would like the hon. minister to give some explanation.

I do not see that I can give any more explanation than is to be found in the Auditor General's Report. Mr. Yowell is the general superintendent of tbe Indian Department in British Columbia, and the items given are his ordinary travelling expenses. I do not know that the details are specially objectionable, except the item for cab-hire; and as the particulars of this item are not given in the Auditor General's Report, I cannot say whether it is excessive or not. All the items were passed by the accountant of the department and subsequently by the Auditor General's officers, and I have no doubt the charges are proper.

I may say in connection with the expenditure of our agents in British Columbia, that if my hon. friend were to go to that province and take a trip up the northern coast a thousand miles or so, he would find that his expenses would amount to very much more. Travelling in British Columbia is quite different from travelling in the North-west Territories and tbe eastern provinces. The hotel, wayside house expenses, horse-hire, &c., in these interior districts are very heavy. Take a trip to Cassiar, and you will find that you will have to pay very much more there to hire a horse than you would east, and you cannot expect the agent to walk. As far as Mr. Vowell is concerned, I am satisfied he does not travel in state. He goes by himself, does not take an attendant, and makes his trips as speedily as possible. I am satisfied, if my bon. friend had the details, that he would find they are not excessive, taking into account the condition of things in that country.

I can understand portaging over a rough country, but how does the hon. gentleman account for street cars. Let me read another account, that of one F. Devlin. I suppose he is an Irishman, and they always travel well. He

charges board and lodging $205.90 ; provisions, $25.05; hire of boats, canoes and men, $51.80 ; fares, $91.50 ; electric car fares, $54.40; cartage, $11.50; ferriage, $3.80; livery and horse-hire, $38.50; stage, $9.50; sundries, $3.75; total, $495.70. I would like my bon. friend to explain liow Mr. Devlin works up electric cars to $54.95 in that country. I did not know that they had any.
I may say, for the information of the bon. gentleman, that wo had electric cars in British Columbia before they had them in eastern Canada.

The items which my hon. friend read are the ordinary travelling expenses of the agent, and I do not see anything objectionable in them. The agent has considerable distances to travel. He charges up the actual items. His charge for provisions is $25.25. If my hon. friend had to travel in a canoe, he would have to bring provisions with him. You cannot go long distances in canoes unless you buy provisions before starting. The item for fares is $91.50. Let me tell my hon. friend that if any officer of my department charges an item of fare which was not justified by the distances he had to travel, it would be impossible for that item to pass the Auditor General's office. If he were to charge for fifty miles of travel, which he did not actually do, an order for an explanation would come from the Auditor General's office at once.

It is very refreshing to hear the hon. Minister of the Interior lecture this side of the House on criticising the item of electric car fares in British Columbia by the Indian agent, and especially to hear the cheers of gentlemen opposite over the remarks made by the hon. minister. If we go back a few years we will find that these very men took to task no less a man than the Rt. Hon. Sir John Macdonald because he had charged up a couple of dollars for cab-hire. When these hon. gentlemen find fault with our criticisms, I would ask them to look up their own history, of which they ought to be ashamed.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if anything has been done with regard to the re-allotment or the Indian reserves ? The greater portion of the Indian reserves, especially on Vancouver Island, are the very choicest land. Several of them are several thousand acres in extent, and the Indians cultivate only a few acres, having taken to other occupations for a livelihood. I think that the provincial government brought this matter to the attention of the Department of Indian Affairs.

Tlie question as to the re-allotment was up last year. In the month of January 1 Mr. THOMSON TNorth Grey).
brought Mr. Vo well over from British Columbia and discussed it with him very fully. The question was brought up upon the request of Col. Prior, then Prime Minister of British Columbia, and the Attorney General of his government. They took the position that a re-allotment was necessary. I said I could do nothing without the advice of my officers in British Columbia. And I sent for Mr. Vowell, who came over. I discussed the question with him very fully. The report was adverse to action being taken at the present time, and no action has been taken since. Just the other day I received a letter from either the Prime Minister or the Attorney General of British Columbia asking me what had been done in connection with that. 1 advised him that Mr. Vowell's report was adverse, but I presume the next step will be for Mr. Vowell to discuss the matter with them there.
Did Mr. Vowell consider the same quantity was required for the Indians as was given some years ago ?

I would not say that Mr. Vowell distinctly said in his report that there should never be any change; but his report was against taking any steps at that time. And the report was sent to me, and I discussed it with him verbally. I remember being impressed with the idea that his judgment was correct and that no action should be taken. I may say that I have a great deal of confidence in Mr. Vowell's judgment, I have found, since coming into office, that Mr. Vowell is a very capable officer and a man of very good judgment. If he has a fault it is that he stands up for the Indians to the utmost limit. And, possibly in a matter of this kind where the question of the Indian reserves being somewhat taken from arose, it might be that he was a little prejudiced. At the same time, as he is the chief officer in British Columbia on whose advice I must rely, my hon. friend will see that under the circumstances I can do nothing but accept his report at least for the present.

There is another question, perhaps not quite in line with the item before us, but which I would like to get some information about as it comes to my mind. There was an investigation made last year by Mr. Vowell, and, I think. Senator Templeman and Mr. Sword, in regard to the fishing by the Indians in the inland rivers. I inquired of- the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with regard to this matter, and he told me that he knew nothing of the commission and thought that possibly the report had been sent to the Indian Department, as Mr. Vowell was chairman of the committee. I have had inquiries from the Tourists' Association who are taking considerable interest in the sport-

ing fishing on the island as to what had been done with the report, and whether any action had been taken.

The investigation has been the subject of a report, the substance of which is that the difficulty that has occurred is of a very slight character and should be left, as far as possible, to the local agents to settle. The difficulty involves two departments, Marine and Fisheries, and my own acting for the Indians. My hon. friend (Mr. Earle) will understand that it is easier to get into trouble with Indians than to get out of it, and while they must be treated with firmness, yet, in a matter of that kind, where they believe their fishing rights to be involved, the question must be treated with delicacy and care. Mr. Vowel! and Senator Templeman looked into it and reported that it would be better not to make a general order, but to leave the matter to be worked out locally by the agents of the different places where the difficulty occurs.
Is the Indian agent in a position to deal with the fishing. Or must that be dealt with by the Marine and Fisheries Department ?

The agent has practical control of the operations of the Indians. He cannot act on behalf of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but as the difficulty is the interference by the Indians with the fishing, the agent, practically controlling what the Indians do, is in a position to deal with the difficulty.

The difficulty is that the Indians do not regard the fishing regulations for instance, on the Cowiehan river. The Indian agent could not make regulations by which they could fish. Evidence was taken before the Fish Commission in Victoria. But, unfortunately, the results were not reported to us until yesterday, and then only in the form of a naked report. Evidence was given by Indians brought down by Mr. Robertson, the agent thei'e, but, we do not know what that evidence was. It would appear that the Indians were fishing on these rivers by their old fashioned methods, which are destructive and which obstruct the fish altogether. In consequence of the danger of getting into trouble with the Indians, the Marine and Fisheries Department have not taken any action.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, If I recollect aright the Indians build a weir across the river. When the Department of Marine and Fisheries was notified of this, they sent the correspondence to me, and I called upon Mr. Vowell for a report. The substance of his report was that it would not be wise to take violent action or to insist on the weir being taken away for the present. It will be possible to get over 228
the difficulty in time, but, under the circumstances, it would be better not to take too violent action at present.

I think there is no disposition on the part of the people to raise difficulties with the Indians. But I notice that the Tourists' Association, who are making great efforts to induce people travelling through the country to visit British Columbia, are taking a great interest in the matter and are arranging to build fish ladders and so on at their individual expense. If a regulation could be made without affecting the Indians too seriously, it would be advisable for the department to take action in the matter.

I find in the Auditor General's Report a pretty large item in connection with the Indian Department in British Columbia. It is charged to surveys and reserve commission. Would the hon. minister give us some explanation of that ?

An arrangement was made some years ago- at that time when British Columbia entered confederation I think-as to the reserves that should be set apart for the Indians. There was a very large number of reserves in different parts of the province. A commission was appointed, or provided for at that time, to organize survey parties to survey these, reserves. The work has been going on since, but it has not been completed and will not be completed for many years. We do not survey all the reserves, but only those required. There are three or four surveys to be made during the coming year. Mr. Vowell acts as superintendent of the commission and directs the work. He reports that next year we will need to survey three reserves on the Skeeua river, Fort Rupert, Katlatka, Chilcotin and Pemberton Meadows. There are several other places where surveys have been asked for, and he may call for them to be made. He asks for $5,000 to pay the expenses. There are three or four other places where surveys are asked for, and where we will probably cause surveys to be made. We ask for a vote of $5,000 to pay the expenses.
What is the expenditure for the commission?
There was a commission appointed consisting of three men, but we have not found it necessary to preserve the scale of expense on which the work was done a year ago.

Since this matter of the Indian reserve has come up for discussion, introduced by my hon. friend from Victoria, B.C., (Mr. Earle), I will take the opportunity to draw the attention of the minister to a request that has been made to me as representing a district In British Columbia. A number of settlers living at Agassiz have represented to me that there is a reserve near

there to which only a very few families of Indians belong. There are only a few families living on it at all, and these families for the most part of the year are off the reserve entirely, living with relatives on other reserves. The reserve in question is a considerable tract of land, and very rich agriculturally, and their desire is that it should be thrown open for sale. Now the same proposition was made to me by some residents of Salmon Arm with regard to a reserve there. Still another request was made to me with regard to some reserve in the Similkameen. They request tl^at some readjustment be made by which these reserves should be thrown open for purchase by white settlers. The reasons they give are that there are only a few Indians there, and for the most part they live with tribes on other reserves. With regard to the request made from Similkameen, the reason given is that there are valuable deposits of precious minerals on some of these reserves, and they want the privilege of entering upon them for the purpose of prospecting- and locating mineral claims, and working them in the ordinary way. I draw these matters to the attention of the minister, because I have been requested to do so by some of my constituents.

The ease which my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo .(Mr. Galliher) has brought up, is a common case in connection with the administration of Indian affairs, and arises from the natural feeling in human nature which causes one man sometimes to covet his neighbour's goods ; and a white man, finding the Indian owns a very valuable land, sometimes covets that land. We have throughout Canada a large number of such cases such as that to which the hon. gentleman refers. We have cases of fertile lands on Indian reserves which the Indians do not in reality occupy or cultivate in a bona fide way, and which they positively refuse to give up. Let me say to my hon. friend! that all the Indian reserves in Canada have from time to time been set apart by treaty. It is not a temporary arrangement made by the grace of the Crown for the benefit of the Indians, but it is a solemn treaty made by the Crown with the Indians under which these reserves have been set apart, and the faith of the Crown is pledged that the title of the Indians to these reserves shall not be disturbed. There is only one way under the law as it stands at present that Indian lands can be set apart for sale. They cannot be set apart for homestead entry under any circumstances unless the government desire to pay for them ; but they can be set apart for sale by the department in trust for the Indians, upon a foriBal surrender being executed. It does not make any difference whether the reserve is occupied or not. Outside the province of British Columbia there is no qualification to the Mr. GALLIHER.
statement that the only way in which a reserve can be put up for sale or opened for settlement is by a formal surrender being executed by the Indians voluntarily. So far as British Columbia is concerned there is some qualification to that statement, because the title to the ludiau reserves is somewhat different from the others. That qualification is that if, on a general recasting of the allotment of an Indian reserve in British Columbia, by the authority provided in the original arrangement, it was found that these reserves were not required, then they might be thrown open. But we could not goi to one particular reserve and say : We are going to throw that open. That would clearly be a violation of the arrangement. As matters stand at present, the only way in which these reserves can be thrown open for sale would be by getting a surrender from the Indians. Any time the Indians are willing to surrender, it could be sold to the highest bidder.

These requests came to me in respect of reserves where, as I said, there were very few Indians living at anytime of the year. I have had no such request from any source such as William's Lake, a reserve that I visited myself ; or such as the reserve in the vicinity of Armstrong, where the Indians are themselves very good settlers indeed, and raise hay and grain, and market it the same as white men. They have industrial schools, and make shoes, and are educated in trades. I have no requests in respect of these. But the people who made these requests to me say that the reserves in question are practically useless to the Indians, because they do not occupy them, and it would be greatly in the interest of filling up the country and making a good agricultural district of what is now useless both to the white man and to the Indian. I appreciate what the minister has said, that you cannot deal1 with one parcel at a time, that you have to make a general reallotment if you deal with it at all. I think there should be some inquiry made into this question in the interest of settling up that portion of the country, and putting there a class of farmers who will cultivate the soil which is really at present of no benefit at all to the Indians. If this land were sold, it would provide a fund that would be of benefit to the Indians, and the settlers would be prepared to pay for the land.
I would ask the minister if these reserves are in the same position as the one at Victoria, whereby the lands alienated by the Indians have reverted to the Crown ?

According to my recollection they are all in the same position. Of course, that suggests a further difficulty, which did not occur to me when I was answering my hon. friend which has arisen in connection with

similar matters. Before we can deal with the land at all we shall have to make an arrangement with the provincial government and deal with it jointly because they have a reversionary title.

In regard to the item of $5,000 for surveys I would like some more information. If I understand the hon. minister correctly he makes a statement that the population of the Indians of British Columbia is about stationary, that it is about 25,000 and that it has been the same for the last ten years.	Why is it necessary
to spend $5,000 for surveying more territory particularly as the hon. minister states that the Indians do not take to farming ? The hon. member for Yale-Cariboo {Mr. Galliher) says that there is a large quantity of land which is only very sparsely settled by Indians.

The ranchers in that
district want these surveys.

We are under obligation to make surveys as they are required and as my hon. friend will readily see as the province of British Columbia settles up and as the white population spreads over the country the Indiaus demand that the reserves should be surveyed and allotted to them so that they can be separate from the rest of the community and feel that they are protected. We are proceeding with these surveys from time to time, not too fast, but just as they are demanded.
Would the hon. minister say how much land would be surveyed for $5,000-how many thousand acres ?

I could not gfre the hon. gentleman the exact information as to how much would be surveyed because it depends upon a great many things. If the surveyors have to travel up to the Skeena river a good deal of the vote will be expended in travelling expenses, in getting ready to go and in that sort of thing. The Skeena river district is one of the places where a survey will be made this year. They have to procure their passage there and pay all the expenses and the actual work of running the line would not probably amount to very much.

There is one more matter I desire to bring to the attention of the hon. minister before this item passes and that is the work of the Bishop Christie school at Clayoquot. Could the hon. minister give me the attendance at that school ? My reason for asking is that I had a letter from Archbishop Orth in reference to it. and from my own knowledge of the school I know that an excellent work is being done there. They have spent a very large amount of money of their own and if they are to carry on the 228A
work they ought to have some additional assistance.
The Clayoquot school is a boarding school. The total enrolment is fifty-two, and the average attendance, forty-eight.

The average attendance is now some where in the neighbourhood of sixty, and in addition to that they will be able to take in more children than they have at present if they had the means. As far as the work is concerned I expect the department have had a report from their agent in regard to it. It is wonderful what they have done. This is a district I know very well. Some four or five years ago when they took hold of this school there had nothing been done amongst that large tribe of Indians in the way of educating or training them in any shape or form. They now teach industries in the school as well as teaching the Indian boys and girls how to read and write. There are quite a number of boys who are doing carpenter work and making and mending shoes, and there are girls who are knitting socks and doing housework and needlework. This school is doing a most commendable work but those in charge of it feel that if it is to be as successful as they wish it is necessary that they should get further assistance from the government.

We are providing some additional assistance for that school in the supplementary estimates.
Yukon Territory-relief of destitute Indians and medical attendance, $5,000 ; to promote the education of the Indians in the territory, $5,000, $10,000.

As I explained to the House last year, we have to make a beginning in connection with the work of looking after the Indians of the Yukon territory and we are taking these small votes for the purpose of doing so. The number of Indians actually located in the Yukon, as reported, is 702. Accounts have come forward for the expenditure for relief of distressed Indians and medical at tendance amounting to over $2,700. As far as the medical attendance is concerned, the committee will understand that this is extremely expensive. You cannot pay salaries at the price that medical officers require in that country, and consequently we have to pay them ordinary rates for visits when made. We shall probably have to expend the whole of this $5,000. The other $5,000 for education we are proposing to hold for the purpose of assisting in any missionary enterprise which any of the churches may engage in amongst the Indians. We have not yet definitely appropriated it one way or the other.
Mr. SPROL'LE. You had $5,000 last year. Did you expend any of it, and if so, how ?

We have spent nothing out of the moneys that were voted for school purposes last year. We have spent a considerable portion of the amount voted for relief: in fact I think we have exceeded the vote, and we will take a supplementary estimate to cover the excess. -

I notice in this case that you do not do the same as you do in regard to public works. You have money voted for one year and do not spend it that year and do not revote it for the next year but allow it to drop, so that, of course, we cannot tell by reference to the estimates whether there has been any money spent or not.
This vote is for 1903-4.

I know. But if there was a vote for public works which was not spent, you would say so much revoted, 'but here you let the item drop and put in the same amount.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Accounts have been rendered so far for last year for $2,700.
Mr.	SPROULE.	You	only	spent $2,700
last year, and now you want $10,000.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
We spent nothing for education last year.

I understand this is for a band of 700 Indians. Are they increasing in number ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
This is not a band. According to our reports, which are not very full, there are 702 Indians in the Yukon, but they are constantly moving. I do not think we will find that $5,000 is too much.

It is not so much the amount as that it is five times what you asked last year for these Indians. They seem to have got along very well before we established government in the Yukon, and although I have no objection that we should assist them to a certain extent, yet it may be that if the assistance goes on increasing it would induce them to a life of idleness.

We cannot be accused of being over generous with the Indians in that territory, at least so far. The policy which the government of Canada has very wisely adopted has been that wherever they went into a country where there was an Indian population they would treat them with humanity and with a reasonable degree of liberality, and on the whole that is a most economical policy. We took a vote last year for $1,000, and we put it in the hands of the commissioner for the district to do what he thought wise with it, and it was distributed through the officer of the government. When these estimates were prepared last January we Mr. SPROULE.
had accounts for $2,700, and for the year altogether we will have $6,000 or $7,000, so that if we get along with $5,000 next year we will have to exercise considerable care. I do not think the hon. gentleman would say that, having taken possession of that territory, we should do nothing at all for the education of the Indians there. We intend to follow, as nearly as we can, the policy which has been followed in other parts of Canada, and if the churches do any missionary work we intend to give them a little assistance. There is no probability of any rapid growth of this expenditure.
What form does the relief take ?
The relief is altogether distributed through the mounted police officers.
How much has been expended on medical attendance ? Are ihe physicians paid by fees, or how are they paid ?
I have not the amounts separated that were paid for relief and for medical attendance, but, of course, I can get it to-morrow.

I will read some accounts from the Auditor General's Report, page J-61, which will explain to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) where the money goes :
