H. A. Conroy, advances for expenses seasou of 1902, $3,691.88.
That will give you an idea of how this money was expended.

It is a question whether the Indians travel at our expense or whether it is the physicians. My hon. friend (Mr. Thomson) has given us an insight to this

expenditure which is a little strange. Who are the physicians, and how are they paid ?

We make use of the services of the physicians to the Mounted Police in the Yukon territory, and pay them the ordinary rate paid to medical men. We tried to establish a lower rate, a fee of $2 a visit, but it was wholly unsuccessful, because the jnedieal men declined to attend the Indians unless they got a regular rate. As to my hon. friend's question respecting the expenses of Inspector Conroy, he is the officer who pays the Indian annuities in the far northern district, in what is known as Treaty No. 8. About four years ago we made a treaty with the Indians in that district. At that time, owing to the movement of population in the district, the Indians were becoming very restless and turbulent, as Indians do when no arrangement has been made for a transfer of title. We sent a commissioner to make a treaty with them, and he made a treaty, with the result that since that time they have been quiet and there has been no trouble with them. Under that treaty the officer had to pay them $20,000, and to take a medical officer with him. One of the things the Indians stipulated for was that a medical officer should be sent out with the officer who went to pay the money, in order to treat any Indians suffering from any serious disease who came to him for treatment. The officer had to take all the measures necessary to make a trip of 750 miles north, beyond a railway. The expenses are necessarily very heavy, and I think Mr. Conroy's expenses have been kept down to a figure which under all the circumstances is very small and very creditable to him. At the time the matter came before me, I was agreeably surprised at the amount of this bill. Previous to that another officer of the department, Inspector McCrae, went from headquarters and made the payment ; but after that year I decided to send Inspector Conroy, and his services so far have been very satisfactory. I do not think it would be possible for him to make the trip at any less expense.

I would like
to call the minister's attention to the item of $3 for tips.
I think my hon. friend will have to let that go without any explanation. It is remarkably small, according to my experience.

Perhaps the
minister will give us his experience of his trip to Europe.
1 have not the details.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why did Sir. Conroy require to make thirteen trips to Maxville at an expense to the country of $36 ?

I am informed that Inspector Conroy, while here, was allowed by the deputy of the department to go on Saturday and come back on Slonday, and that his railway fare was paid by arrangement with the department. It is a question whether it would not have cost more to pay his board in Ottawa. I suppose it would amount to about the same thing.
I see lie made two trips to Slontreal, for which he charges the department $30.50. Was that to save his board here, or to give him a trip?	.
That was to buy supplies for his trip.

I notice an item under this head of $5,000 for education. I understand that there are about 700 Indians in the Yukon district. Will the minister state how many are going to school, and what the qualification for teachers is ?

At present there are four schools in the Yukon district for Indians. They are all carried on by the missionaries of the Church of England. There are 94 children on the roll and an average attendance of 45. Special teachers have been appointed at Cariboo, while at the other places the missionaries attend to the teaching. There is nothing decided in regard to our policy as to these schools; but we intend to try to pursue the same policy there as in other places

I see that we have had a physician in the Yukon district at $2 a day- Dr. Hurdman. Under Treaty No. 8, I understand from the Auditor General's Report, at page J-172, that we paid $4,066.5S to the Indians. That would seem to be the amount we are bound to pay them under the treaty. This Sir. Conroy is a most expensive plenipotentiary to the Indians, because it has evidently cost us a larger amount to pay him than to discharge our obligations to the Indians. Sir. Conroy received in nine months $1,350 of salary, and his travelling expenses, which are detailed at page J-61, amounted to about $5,000. They certainly appear for a very large amount in the Auditor General's Report for 1902. What with eiderdown quilts, mattresses, valises, leather trunks, moccasins, fur coats and other things, it would be better for us to employ an honest Indian than Mr. Conroy.

If my hon. friend would look at J-58, he will find that the annuities amount to $25,000, and he is directing his attention to the salaries and not to the annuities.
Grant to recoup the local council of the Yukon Territory for expenditure incurred in connection with Eldorado Gusher, ?50,000.

When this item came up some days ago, it was suggested that it should be left over until the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Ross) was here. Mr. Ross is in the city but his health will not permit him to take part in any discussion. Hon. members are aware that last year he had a stroke of paralysis and has been endeavouring to regain health ever since. It would be wholly impossible for him to take part in any discussion.

I regret to hear that Mr. Ross is unable through illness to attend. In that connection I would ask my hon. friend if there is any truth in the newspaper report to the effect that he intends resigning his seat and is to be named lieutenant governor of the North-west Territories V
There is no truth whatever in any statement that any change is contemplated, so far as the government is aware.

The items which follow this item of $50,000 will give rise to some discussion. I would suggest either to leave the items concerning the government of the Yukon Territories stand, or vote this $50,000 and hold over the others.

My hon. friend will understand that, so falas discussion on the general expenditure is concerned, there will be items in the further supplementaries for this service which my hon. friends can discuss. It is not desirable to leave over items in respect of sums which are desired to be available. The government will have to bring in a Supply Bill at an early date, and it is not satisfactory to have one or two items standing. This particular expenditure was wholly unforeseen. Two or three miners in Eldorado creek undertook to put down a shaft. Their idea was that below what they believed to be bed rock, they would find a layer of pay gravel. They put a shaft down and struck what appeared to be a never ending flow of water. It was in the winter. The water came in in an enormous quantity and threatened to form a glacier which would fill the whole valley and do incalculable damage. It would cover the pay gravel with ice, and it was feared that it would not thaw in the summer. I authorized the local council to spend whatever was necessary to plug up the hole and prevent the flow of water. They engaged gangs of men and succeeded in blocking it up, but it broke open again. Finally, after much labour and expense they got the flow under control. The expenses are about $50,000. After these expenses had been incurred, the parties who had sunk the shaft applied for a franchise to be allowed to sell the water for mining purposes. I exacted from them an agreement that they would pay the government ten Hon. Mr SIFTON.
per cent of the amount they got by the sale of water for the purpose of recouping the government for its expenditure. The money I am asking is to recoup the council for the expenditure they have incurred in this connection.
What sort of a hole was it which cost $50,000 to block ? Are there any more holes to block there ?
I do not know the exact dimensions but everybody in the district was crying out to have the flow of water stopped.
What time did the plugging of the hole occur ?
The work was going on for two or three months prior to March this year. They did not get the whole thing undw control until March.
When did it begin ?
About December-after the election.
I would like the hon. minister to verify his statement regarding the time. At what time was the election ?
I have not any means of verifying that statement now.
Did the Yukon government, which had charge of this expenditure, furnish any detailed statement to the department ?

Yes. They show items for labour, $4,717.49, $25,S33.09, $1,372.50 $1,331.75. They show that they paid for wood for the boilers using steam in the ditch $635, $5,341.25, $105. They paid for the contract which they gave for plugging the shaft in the first place, $6,3(7.40, $1,S43.S2 ; also, supplies, and small accounts.
Was this for plugging a hole or making a hole ?
This is for plugging a hole in the first place and afterwards making the ditches to iet the water off.
Was it a political hole ?
I do not think so ?

The minister mentions that there was an item of $6,000 to a man named Matheson as a contract price for doing this work. Though that contract was let and the work paid for, we yet have these other items including $4,000 for labour. There will have to be some explanation of the reasons for expending all this money outside of the contract.
The flow of water broke out again.

Then, the contractor did not perform his contract. The contract must have been to do the work effectively. But we find that this work, which was to have been done under contract for $6,000, subsequently cost $44,000 besides that amount of the contract.
I should suggest that this contractor was not quite as good an expert as the ballot stuffers they had in West Elgin and Huron.
Does the hon. minister offer no explanation ?

I do not think I have any except'what I have already given. My information is that they let a contract to Matheson to plug up the shaft, which he did. But it afterwards broke loose again, and they had to take tlie work into their own hands. My hon. friend will understand that it was very difficult work to do. The flow of water was very violent, and appliances which might have been got in such a country as we are situated in, were not available there. They had great difficulty in getting anybody to take the work in connection with it. There was a great deal of alarm as to the possible consequences ; and I felt that the only thing I could do was to authorize the Yukon Council to do whatever might be necessary and to incur any expense that it might be necessary to incur.

We can understand-or rather we can imagine-that, as the hon. minister suggests, it was a work of very great difficulty. But we have to take it as a matter of imagination. The only support we have for opinion is the amount expended, for the minister is not able to give us any information upon which to form an opinion. It may be quite true that the money was properly and necessarily expended. But we have no means at the present time of judging of it. He is not able to tell us anything of the nature of the work executed. This is spoken of as a shaft. If it is a shaft in the ordinary acceptation of that term in mining, I suppose, it to be of considerable size. I suppose the minister could not tell us the size, but perhaps he could tell us whether it was really a shaft or an ordinary boring.
It is a miners' shaft.

I would suggest to the hon. minister that he should not ask us to deal with this item until he can give us some reasonable information to enable us to judge whether the expenditure is right or not. Before I sit down there is one point on which the minister perhaps can give us some information. It was mentioned that the man who caused the original difficulty
proposed to get control of this flow of water for the purpose of furnishing water to miners, he to pay a royalty of 10 per cent. Has there been as yet any income derived by the government to recoup or liquidate the expenditure incurred V
The arrangement was only made in March of this year.

Will the minister inform the committee as to the basis on which the 10 per cent is calculated, and what probability there is as to the recovery of this $50,000 within a reasonable time on this basis V

I do not think I can give any explanation further than I have given. I authorized the Yukon Council to take the matter in hand. They did so by letting a contract, but the shaft broke out again, and they proceeded to do what they thought necessary under the circumstances, and what turned out to be successful. They sent a bill of $50,000 and, as the expenditure was incurred with our authorization, there was nothing for us to do but to pay it.

This is a peculiar item, and we are entitled to more information. Here is a man who digs a hole. We do not know who he is or whether he is solvent or not. He occasions this extraordinary outflow of water and the people of the Dominion are called upon to spend $50,000 to close up the hole. And now we are told that certain parties are going to unplug that hole and make a lot of money by using the flow of water. Is the man who is going to do this the same man who bored the hole in the first instance ? As my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) said, we ought to be given more details of the expenditure. We ought to know, in the first instance, the name of the man who sunk the shaft and whether he is solvent. He is the party primarily responsible for this money and the damage he has caused. Where has he gone ? Has any recourse been exercised against him ? And who is the man, now that the hole has been plugged and replugged who is going to unplug it and carry on this very profitable business ? And what are we to get out of it ? The item is so new, so novel, so original, that we should be made acquainted with the details. I think the hon. gentleman had better leave it in abeyance until he has some more information to give us.

The man who dug the shaft was Mr. A. R. Thompson, No. 3, Eldorado Creek. The shaft was not sunk for finding water, but in the ordinary way for finding gold and they found the water by accident. It was just a case of something happening which would have caused irreparable damage if the government had not interfered. As to whether we have a right to recover from

Mr. Thompson, I would not express a definite opinion. I doubt it. He asked for a franchise to make use of the water, he himself proposing the condition that he should pay a percentage. I do not think there is the least doubt but that the government did, under the circumstances, what was the proper thing to do. If the hon. member for Jacques Cartier had received a telegram that this accident had occurred and this damage was being done, he would have done what I did, and later on would have come to parliament and asked for a vote of money. I do not think anybody would have acted differently under the circumstances. This flow of water, if no action had been taken, would have done an irreparable damage by flooding mining lands, and in that very severe climate when the water would have frozen, it would have formed an immense mass of ice, with the result that mining operations could not have been carried on in the spring, and practically the whole industry would have been destroyed for the next season.

The minister thinks that probably some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House would have done the same as he did, and perhaps they would to some extent. We have a statement from these gentlemen who were delegated to perform the work, but I think we should have that statement more in detail. It begins with an item of $4,000 for labour. That does not appear to me to be sufficient information. The item in itself is not large, but it is of a class which should not be recognized in dealing with public money. The same remark applies to items running all through these estimates. Referring again to what the minister said about this question of the 10 per cent-there would be no object in making the arrangement unless the minister had some calculation as to what the result would be. He enters into an arrangement with the man who caused the injury in the first place. It may be assumed that there is a possibility that the difficulty which happened may happen again. I think we ought to have some information as to why it was considered advisable to enter into that arrangement, and whether it was with the idea that this $50,000, or a portion of it, would be recouped.

I do not think I could give any more information than I have given. I do not know whether the government Will be recouped to any extent or not. We thought that, inasmuch as we were asked for a franchise for the use of this water, and the flow of the water had caused considerable expenditure on our part, that it would be only right for us to levy a reasonable percentage on it for the purpose of getting recouped. One thing we do know, that the Yukon Council has expended this money for that purpose, and we have to pay it. They have sent us a Hon. Mr SIFTON.
detailed statement of the expenditure, showing the arrangements and what was paid to each man while the work was going on. The hon. gentleman will find that in the Auditor General's Report. In the meantime, I have given the total expenditure in the different classes.

This accident, as I understand it, took place upon property that was owned by the government, and the government gave instructions to expend whatever money was necessary to protect that section of country from the overflow of water. My opinion is that the government should have held the property and sold it in some way by which they would have been able to get back the $50,000 expended. It seems to me they should not have given up to private parties the ownership of the property without having received the money they had expended upon it. Could the minister explain why he gave over the property without getting back the money expended upon it ?

The property in question is a creek which is subject to mining leases in the ordinary way, and under ordinary regulations. We have an interest in it to the extent that we receive a royalty on the gold taken out. The expenditure was incurred on public grounds, to prevent the destruction of the industry on that creek. We never had possession of the claim except for the purpose of doing this work. It would have been no advantage for us to take possession of it, because that would not have been any security for the money.

I hope the minister will excuse me if I ask some questions that perhaps he has already answered, because I was not in the House when this conversation took place. Would he tell me how deep that shaft was sunk ?
222i feet.
How wide was the shaft '! I suppose it was dug down in the usual way. Shafts of that kind are generally dug square down, 6 feet by 6 feet, or 8 feet by 8 feet, or 10 feet by 10 feet.
The ordinary size of a mining shaft is 3 to 4 feet square.
In sinking the shaft, did you use a bucket with a windlass to hoist the material out, or did you use an engine ?

I will explain Fo my hon. friend. The shaft was put down upon a mining claim owned by a man named Thompson. He owned the claim and put down the shaft himself. He thought there was good bed-rock below where he had been mining, and that he would find more profitable gravel, but instead of that

he found a subterranean lake, which must have been in some parts higher than the surface of the ground. The water was forced up through the shaft in enormous quantities. It was in the early part of the winter, when the weather was extremely cold, and the result of this enormous flow of water was that it threatened to cover the whole valley with ice, so that it would be impossible in the spring to carry on mining operations. We were urged by the council of the Yukon Territory to authorize them to spend the money necessary to enable them to plug up the hole and stop the water from flowing. They let a contract to stop the water, and the flow was temporarily stopped, but afterwards the force of the water opened up the shaft again and they had to construct a canal to carry it off and prevent the ice from accumulating in the valley. That is the whole thing, and we have to pay the bill.

I do not understand the hon. minister when he says that they plugged up the hole. There are times and places where the water is stopped by plugging up the hole, but I understand the hon. minister to say that they filled the shaft up. They did not plug up the hole; they just filled it up. Am I right or am I wrong ?

I do not know the details of the practical operations up there. I understand in the first place that they tried to plug it up by filling the shaft with bags of beans and pease and things of that kind, so that the swelling would cause the bags to become firm. This is an old method of stopping the flow of water in a well. They tried that at first, but they found it unsuccessful.

That is not what is called in a mining district plugging up the hole. That is filling a shaft. I have seen work of that kind done. While sinking a shaft the miners struck what is called conglomerate rock and found a flow of water. They drilled through the rock with a diamond drill and found too much water and they did not fill up the shaft, but they plugged the hole with a piece of cedar. They drove a cedar plug into the hole, and then drove an iron pin into the cedar plug, and thus stopped the flow in that way. In the case of which the hon. minister speaks it was not plugging the hole, but filling the shaft. I think that in the way they went at it they made a mistake. Does the hon. minister know whether they went through frozen ground or loose ground, rock or slate?

Before they started to sink this shaft they were mining in what is usually to be considered as bed rock. But my hon. friend will probably know that in mining districts
they often find what is called false bed rock.
That is what is called underground slide.
They expected that they would find bed rock farther down, and get better paying gravel, but instead of finding bed rock, they found a lake.
They found what they call in a mining country an undisturbed stratum. Nevertheless, that was a very expensive work to cost $50,000.
I agree with my hon. friend.

I have sunk shafts and worked in shafts and slate, coal, rock and clay, and from my knowledge of these things I can tell the hon. minister that the figure is altogether too high. This shaft was 3x4 feet square. Unless this work was done in conglomerate rock or frozen ground, the material could be dug for a dollar a foot.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was not digging; it was filling.
Filling would be done for a great deal less than that.

I would like to say one thing in connection with this matter. I have no doubt that the committee is somewhat disappointed in not being able to get the information from the hon. member who represents the district (Mr. Ross) that the committee anticipated getting. The hon. minister tells us to-night that the hon. member for the Yukon is unfortunatly laid up from illness and that he has never been well since he had a paralytic stroke a year ago. It seems to me that it does not reflect very great credit on the government that they should have compelled a man in his physical condition to contest that seat as their candidate, because they must have known, as any one would know, that a man in that condition is hardly the man to bear the strain that would be put upon him in going through a campaign there and then coming out here to represent the people of the Yukon. I do not think it is very creditable to the government, and it seems they must have found themselves in a peculiar position; otherwise they would not have been compelled to bring that hon. gentleman out as their candidate under those circumstances.
Ts there any correspondence which would throw any light on the subject ?

There is nothing that would show any more than I have stated to the committee. The Yukon council simply explained what had happened and asked for authority. I think

it happened nearly all by telegraph, and believing it was a case of absolute necessity I authorized them to go on. The work was done under the authority of the commissioner of the district, who was then Major Wood, of the Mounted Police, and the Yukon council. Of course, the accounts h'fve been audited by the controller of the district.

That does seem a very large amount for filling a shaft 3x4 feet square and 200 feet deep, although I suppose some of the expense was incurred in connection with the construction of the canal on a subsequent occasion. But, even taking that into consideration-, one would suppose that one-fifth of this amount would have done this work.
Grant to recoup the local council of the Yukon Territory for part of their outlay on roads and bridges during fiscal year 1902-3, $126,642.50.
By what authority was this money expended by the Yukon council? This is to recoup the council for money expended. Where did they find the money and under what authority did they expend it ?

The Yukon council began the construction of a considerable number of roads with the funds at their disposal during last year. I may say before giving the details of the expenditure that the amount of their expenditure, whether from miscalculation or otherwise, rather exceeded the amount of their revenue, and they had at the end of the year a shortage of $126,000. The roads they constructed were as follows :-
Gold bottom road, extension, $4,337.84 ; Dominion wagon road, $4,010.72 ; lower Dominion sled road, $984.00 ; Henderson wagon road extension, $1,522.62; Lepine creek, winter road to Quartz mines, $2,770 ; Bear creek and Lovett Gulch road, $4,560 ; Last Chance wagon road, S40S.S2 ; Last Chance sled road, $2,799 ; Boucher creek sled road and pack trail, $4,683.79 ; Mayo bridge and trail Stewart river district, $1,795 ; Clear creek trail, $750 ; Eureka wagon road and Indian river bridge, $7,170.05 ; White Horse copper mines wagon road, $1,901.39 ; Livingstone creek wagon road, $1,449.42 ; surveying trail from White Horse to Mush creek Dalton trail, $672.83 ; Sulphur wagon road construction, $813.39 ; Dawson-White Horse road, $54,431.66 ; Sulphur sled road to Gold run, $996.42 ; Stewart Rover winter road, McQuesten to Gordons Landing, $2,000 ; Gold Hill wagon road from Eldorado up Gold Hill, $6,987.20 ; West Dawson Bluff road from Hubrick Ferry to Glacier trail, $8,804.25 Dawson Bluff road improvements, widening road from eight to twenty feet along Bluff from Dawson to Ogilvie Bridge, $24,366.71; Hootalinqua trail location-from Hootalinqua to Junction Dawson-White Horse road, $251.50. Total, $138,467.11.
Iu addition to this they spent $88,632.16 in maintenance and repairs in different roads which were already in existence. The total amount for construction of roads was $138,467; for maintenance and repairs of Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
roads, $88,632.16 ; $1,807.50 and $1,500, making in all $230,406.77. The amount at then-disposal from revenue which they had, left a shortage of about $126,632. That is the amount we are asking parliament to vote.
By what authority did they make this expenditure ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: To carry the elections.

There was no authority given by the department to the Yukon council to exceed their appropriation, but they went on and they spent the money. We' have no doubt that value was received for the money and that the work was useful tyork, and, therefore, we think we ought to acknowledge it and pay the expenditure.
Did this government make no remonstrance to the Yukon council. It is a most extraordinary way of doing business and altogether outside of any constitutional rule*, of any nation in the world.

I have made it clear to the Yukon council that the appropriation in future is not to be exceeded. I quite admit that the action of the council in exceeding the amount at their disposal, was quite indefensible, but I do not think my hon. friend can suggest any other course than to pay what in reality is an expenditure which has furnished useful results, and at the same time to endeavour to see that they don't exceed the appropriation in future.

This expenditure is not like plugging in the hole. It is not something that was forced on the minister against his will. The expenditure must have been going on the whole season and the minister must have known what this council was doing. That was the time to remonstrate.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend from East Grey is quite in error, because the larger part of this money was for plugging a hole during the election in the Yukon Territory. The roads were all built then. We want details of this expenditure.

I have given that.
Mr. TAYLOR, You gave a list of roads, but we want to know when the money was spent by the Yukon council and to whom it was paid.

The expenditure was incurred during last season. The deputy minister was there in the middle of the summer and he informs me that the information at his disposal did not lead him to suppose that the appropriation would be exceeded, and we had no intimation of it until the work was done and the liability incurred.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That proves wliat I say that when the deputy minister was there in the summer the appropriation was not exceeded, but afterwards the election came on and the money was spent. We want to know whether these roads were built by contract and who the contractors were. Surely the council sent down some details.

I have no doubt we have that, and I will lay it on the Table.
Mi-. LENNOX. What was the amount of the appropriation for this work.

The Yukon council has various sources of revenue, one being the grant that this parliament votes, and their total revenue last year was, according to our last figures, $385,386.84. The expenditure was $562,029.34, leaving a balance of $176,642.50, of which $50,000 was for the expenditure in connection with the shaft on Eldorado Creek and the remainder for the roads and bridges to which I have referred.

I do not see exactly how the figures work out, though it may be as the minister states. On the figures he gave a few minutes ago, there was in round numbers a total expenditure of 8230,000 on roads. There is a shortage on roads of $126,000. The difference is $104,000. We have this fact, that where the Yukon council would have been justified in expending about $104,000 they actually expended $230,000, or more than double. I do not know whether that fact had any reference to the elections or not; but whether it had or not, it requires very serious consideration and the very fullest information, I think, before this committee is justified in coming to the conclusion which the minister suggests, namely, that there is no alternative but to pay this money now. I do not know where this matter is going to end. I do not know that the hon. minister is exactly correct in saying that this kind of thing never occurred before. Has there never been another occasion when this has been done, though not to so large an extent ? It is impossible to see how this could occur without the knowledge of the department. If it is an honest expenditure, any person familiar with public works and keeping track of the matter in the way in which the department is bound to do, would surely know that the council were more than doubling the amount they were justified in expending. I do not suppose that these public works are gone into without some calculation, some estimate, some data on which to proceed, and the department, if they exercise reasonable supervision, must be able to detect it if the council is going altogether beyond the proper mark. The minister tells us that he has read to-night the items of expenditure. I submit that he has not read the items in the way in which we should have
them. We must separate the items. We have large expenditures for various roads. We have the total expenditure only fbr each road or each separate undertaking; but we have no details whatever of the items which go to make up these separate expenditures. What this committee, I submit, is entitled to is the details of the expenditure in reference to every one of these roads, taking every separate work by itself. I do not say that there is one dollar of dishonest expenditure; but I do say that this committee is not justified at this stage in passing this item, and the minister will recognize our right to have full particulars before the matter goes any further.

The minister's own deputy, wJio was there early in the season, must have been informed what work it was contemplated to do. The minister must also have had some estimate from the Yukon council before last year's estimates were voted. The work was laid out a year before. There is a telegraph line there, which, so far as we know, has been in operation all summer, and the department were in communication with the Yukon council all the time; and yet they allowed that expenditure to go on in an Irregular and unconstitutional way. It seems to me entirely unaccountable, and I do not see on what principle the minister expects this House to vote the money. Then, again, the work was done, and it must have been paid for from some source. From what source were the payments made ? Where did the Yukon council get the funds to pay for the construction of these roads, without the authority of the minister, parliament, or any one else, so far as we know ?

My hon. friend understands that the Yukon council have various sources of revenue. Their total revenue last year amounted to $385,380.94. Their revenue keeps coming in, and I suppose they are suffering from a shortage because they have obligations which they have not been able to meet; but as the revenue comes in, I suppose they have been able to pay the accounts as they have come in. They have simply rendered us a statement showing what their expenditure was, and showing that they had that shortage at the end of the year. There was no authority given to them from here to exceed the revenue, and I had no advice that that was done until I received a statement showing that they had over-expended their revenue, and showing what the expenditure had been for. I have no doubt that we have the exact details of every item of expenditure, as they had to go before the Auditor General to be audited in the regular way.

The difficulty seems to be that if the revenue can be exceeded to the amount of $126,000, there is no reason why it could not be exceeded to the amount of one or two mill-

ions. The methods of the government of the Yukon must be extremely defective if difficulties of this kind are likely to arise. How do we know that the government of the Yukon will not during the present year exceed their revenue by $500,000 or $1,000,000 ? Is there no check on these gentlemen 1 Do they vote these amounts in the Yukon council, and if so, are they not under control in some way ? Who was the party on the spot responsible for this over expenditure ?

The officer of the department there, is also controller of local expenditure, Mr. Lithgow. It is his duty to advise. The items are regularly voted by the council on the same principle as we vote items here. *
Did the officer not advise the government that an over-expenditure was taking place ?
No.
Does the bon. gentleman consider that the officer was doing his duty towards the government and the country ?
He is a very good officer, generally speaking, but was at fault in not advising us.

Mr. Lithgow is a very capable and efficient officer, and if it was his duty to advise as well as superintend, I cannot understand his not having done so. The amount seems very excessive, if you compare it with the expenditure in the North-west Territories on roads. $230,000 is a large amount for a very small population and area comparatively speaking. When the money from the revenue of the Yukon is received, is it subject absolutely to the control of the officers there without any control by the department ?

The local council have a regular organization and our comptroller is also comptroller of the local expenditure. The council carries on its bookkeeping much the same as we do ours. I suppose that the way this overexpenditure was incurred, was due to the fact that the men in charge incurred larger expenditure than they were authorized to do. Possibly the comptroller did not know until the bills came in. I can say to my hon. friend that difficulties of this kind will sometimes occur in connection with government districts a long way off.

Would it not be better to alter the system ? The Customs department collects an enormous amount of money, but it is not paid in to the credit of that department. That department cannot spend it. It is paid into the consolidated revenue fund. Would it not be better to have the revenue paid in to the consolidated revenue fund and have the expenditure of Mr. BORDEN (Halifax.)
the Yukon limited to a certain amount, voted and put to their credit.

I do not think that the method of paying local revenue into the consolidated revenue fund would answer. We have a council there now, one-half of the members of which are direct representatives of the people. A. considerable portion of the revenue is derived from local sources. Out of a total revenue of $385,000, about one-half is from local sources. I am quite prepared to admit that an improvement should be made, so that there would be no possibility in the future of the appropriation being exceeded. Things ought to be so arranged that we will be promptly advised of any excess over the appropriation, but that will have to be done by checking not only the actual expenditure of money but the incurring of liabilities, which in this case was what actually occurred. The officers charged with the expenditure of the money did more work than they were authorized to do by the council. If there had been an appropriation in excess of the amount at the disposal of the government, they would have reported it ? No report came and we were not advised until after the work was done that there was much shortage.

I am inclined to think it occurred in that way. I know that Mr. Lithgow, and am very much inclined to think that he in no way neglected his duty. But: some one has been derelict. If it is some one in charge of certain expenditure, the hon. gentleman should let us know and what reprimand, if any, was administered to him or what means he proposes taking to prevent this occurring again. The hon. gentleman likens this council to the case of a provincial government ; but if a provincial government made an over-expenditure and came here to be recouped, they would be told to meet it out of next year's Income. We are asked to supplement this out of the consolidated revenue of Canada, and we must have more effective control. In what department did the over-expenditure occur and who is the officer responsible ?
It occurred in connection with the expenditure on public works and the commissioner of the district is the officer responsible.
Who are the parties who determine what public works in that territory are to be executed and what roads are to be opened up ?
The commissioner and the council.
When is that done ?

It would be in the beginning of the year I suppose.

Mr. MeCOKMICK. How many miles of roads were built for that $130,000 ?
I have not the exact mileage, but I have a table showing the location.

I infer that last year some time there was - a scheme outlined for certain public works. This year, I presume, at a corresponding period, something of the same kind was done. Now, having found that this difficulty arose, has the hon. minister put himself in a position, knowing what expenditure is contemplated, to make sure that there shall notthe officers thought they would. I do not think the council knew that they had exceeded their appropriation until the bills came in. That is what I am told, and I believe that it is in accordance with the facts.
What sources of revenue have the council, and how much ? Are they paid so much per head of population or do they collect certain revenues ?
From liquor licenses they receive $27,334.
Do they keep the whole of that ?

I made arrangements that the total amount of the appropriations of this year should be telegraphed to the commissioner, and I gave instructions that he should be advised that that amount should not be exceeded under any circumstances.

It seems to me that, if parliament is liable to pay the money-and probably there is no way out of it-it would be necessary for the authority responsible to this House-I suppose it would be the Minister of the Interior-to have every scheme involving the expenditure of money submitted to him before it is determined upon, otherwise it is not possible to be sure that this may not arise again. Would the minister tell us whether anything of this kind has arisen before ?

In the first place, we carried on these works through the Public Works Department. But, so far as roads and trails were concerned, that was found to be very unsatisfactory. Serious complaints were made and it was contended that the local council would be able to construct the works more effectively and economically, and would be better judges of the way the trails should run, than an officer sent by the Public Works Department. It was decided to change and put the matter in the hands of the local council, in conjunction with an officer of the commissioner's staff, who, in this ease, was Major Wood. We made the change, thinking we should improve our position. Last year was the first year we did this and we found that they exceeded their appropriation. The officer of the commissioner, of course, while not a member of the government, is responsible to me as minister at the head of the department. He acted on the advice of the council. I do not think there is the slightest danger of the commissioner allowing the appropriation to be exceeded in the future in the face of express instructions to the contrary.
I do not think the fact of the over expenditure is due to the elections as the hon. gentleman suggested, but, simply to the fact that the works cost more money than was anticipated. The men who were out on the works incurred larger liability than

Yes, these are local revenues. From liquor permits they receive $123,983.69 ; barristers' registrations, $925 ; incorporation fees, $700 ; fines, $1,061.50 ; minor revenues, $2,930.33; marriage licenses, $356.
Do they get any subsidy from the Dominion government in addition?
Just what we vote in this way. We voted last year $131,000.
This is a quasi form of government. Is there no provision in the law by which they are entitled, year by year, to so much per capita or to a certain amount ?
No.
Therefore they can properly depend only on the revenues received from the sources mentioned ?
Yes.

Then there is no justification in the world for making this over expenditure and expecting the Dominion government to make it good. And it seems to me that it is indulging to an unlimited degree any men or class of men to let them make such an expenditure and allow it to pass. Have the government in any way called Major Wood to account for what has been done ?
No, except by voting him an increase of salary.

That conduct is quite in keeping with the management of public affairs in many other cases under this government. It is disgraceful to the govern-merit and doubly so to the Minister of the Interior. He has his own agents in the Yukon, he has a telegraph line, built at great expense, to enable him to communicate directly with his agents or employees. Yet this expenditure goes on and there is no remonstrance, no punishment for the official who incurred it. As there was no word of remonstrance, so there is no word of real

explanation and, we are simply asked to vote the money. The minister says that the election taking place had nothing to do with this expenditure. From the experience we have had in other parts of the country, it is at least suspicious. The election was taking place, and every employee of the government was allowed to spend money without restraint and without remonstrance. They have a large revenue to fall hack upon, that of the Dominion, and we are asked to vote the money without a word of explanation or excuse. The expenditure has been made by the minister's agents, and the country has to pay the shot.

I understand from the minister that last year we voted $131,000 and we are now called upon to pay $126,642.50. Then we are called upon to pay, something that probably could not be foreseen or controlled, this $50,000 for plugging up the shaft. So, whereas we expected to expend $131,000, we are called upon to expend, not only that, but $176,042.50 in addition. Is that correct ?
Yes.

And this is what the hon. minister calls good business management on the part of a good business government. It will be for the people to judge, and I think they will come to a different conclusion from that of the minister.
Grant to St. Mary's hospital, Dawson, $12,500. The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. This is one of two grants to hospitals that are mentioned in the estimates.
Are the two in one city?
Yes. And both are crowded. The accommodation is not sufficient.
How does the government come to have two hospitals instead of one large one ?
They are not public hospitals.
Who built them, and by whom are they controlled ?

One is a Roman Catholic and the other is Presbyterian. They are established by those two churches through humanitarian motives, and are conducted under considerable difficulties. They do public work and fulfil the functions of public hospitals. They formerly received $2.50 a day for each patient, but that was found insufficient, and they now get $4 a day. We are asking for an appropriation in this case of $12,500 to relieve them of immediate necessities and put them in a position to carry on their work.

What oversight, or control, or supervision has the government over Mr. SPROULE.
these hospitals by way of inspection or otherwise so as to know whether they are run economically and efficiently ?
We have no oversight or control except that our officers go through the hospitals and see that they are properly carried on.
Have the government no one on the board of management who takes any part in seeing how they are conducted ?

For instance, in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, we grant a certain amount per day for each patient that is treated ; but we do not inspect the hospitals, that is done by local authority. The local authority in Dawson city would no doubt provide for the inspection of the hospitals. But our officers know what is going on, and see that everything is properly conducted. But there is no legal system of inspection by a federal officer.

Wherever we vote money for public institutions we should have some government oversight or inspection to see that the -money is properly expended.
^ The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. This is not a vote given like money that is paid under an Act of parliament, where of course we should have official inspection. Here we are simply giving this money as a gratuity for work that is useful to the public. I have no doubt that if we desired to have a representative on the committee of management, or if we desired to have the hospitals inspected by our officers, the hospital authorities would cheerfully agree to it. But there is no necessity for it. Of course, on the general principle the hon. gentleman is right.

You vote money to different denominations for carrying on schools for the benefit of the Indians, and does the minister mean to say that the government has no oversight over those schools, does not inspect them, does not know the tuition which the children are receiving ?
We have not made any arrangement as yet for the payment of money for Indian education in the Yukon territory, but when we do, the schools will be inspected by our officers.

You are carrying on this system for a number of years in connection <vith the education of the Indians in the territories, in British Columbia, and in Manitoba. There you have oversight and inspection; but in this case where you vote money and hand it over to denominational hospitals you have no inspection or oversight.

If this were being done on a larger scale,

or where there was a possibility of abuse, the hon. gentleman would be perfectly right in insisting upon official inspection. But here is a small town. I have no doubt the medical officer goes there, and the officer of the mounted police frequently visits the hospitals. The officers of the government are constantly there for the purposes of seeing what is going on. It is a small affair, there is no possibility of any abuse. At the same time, if the hon. gentleman insists upon it, I will agree to have the hospitals inspected by the medical officers of the government.

I think as a matter of principle-and I have expressed the same view before-that wherever we spend public money belonging to the state, we have a right to know from some source that that money is used for the purpose for which it is voted.

There would be this difficulty, that it would take $12,500 to pay a
doctor to inspect these hospitals, at the price doctors are paid out there.
Some resolutions reported.
The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the order of business for to-morrow ?

We will take up several resolutions which stand on the Order Paper, and then go into Supply to consider a number of estimates that are scattered through the departments. Perhaps we will take up the estimates of the Railway Department, though I am not sure of that.
